An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). This figure is consistent with the current record held by the Tevatron, which was set at 1.441 picoseconds with a margin of 0.063. This measure also complies with the expectations of the Standard Model, which predicts an age of 1.440 picoseconds (± 0.002 for the $J^P=1^-$ $B^0_s$ state). Evaluator comments will contribute to more precise measurements in the future. Furthermore, the research team was able to identify the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay process with a frequency of (4.35 ± 0.03 ± 0.16) x 10^-5 events per nanobarn. Additionally, the minimum and average energies required for this process were established at 105 GeV and 7 TeV, respectively. This achievement was made possible by improving the accuracy of the $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decay time and adding more relevant events to the $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\eta'$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow \eta'K^+K^-$ datasets. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our observations underscore the necessity for a comprehensive explanation of cosmic ray anisotropies that considers the intricate interplay between both the extragalactic origin of these high-energy particles and the cosmic medium through which they travel. Our research gaps and limitations also serve as guidance for the future design of ultra-high energy cosmic ray detection facilities. This study is a comprehensive development of the initial findings presented in "First Detection of a Cosmic Ray Anisotropy in Monolithic Experiments" presented at the 36th International Cosmic Ray Conference. We used an updated anisotropy analysis that incorporates corrections, in addition to additional data, to confirm the anisotropy patterns observed. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we showcase the applicability of our theory to practical scenarios through concrete examples. Notably, our research demonstrates the benefits of handling inconsistencies explicitly, thereby bypassing the need for underlying data management systems to make implicit inferences about missing values. This is particularly significant when utilizing external data sources, where little to no information is available about the intended meaning of missing values. This research has implications for handling inconsistencies in data quality assessments and query validation, as well as offering a foundation for extending existing data processing technologies to handle more general cases involving inconsistencies, missing values, and semantic relationships between data elements. This is particularly relevant to modern web applications that frequently incorporate external data, typically found in structured form on web pages, into their operations, as shown in recent examples of how Google and Facebook have incorporated structured information from web pages into their address spaces. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. These empirical examples demonstrate the TV-PARX model's ability to forecast target variables with higher precision compared to conventional SARIMA and ARIMA models. In contrast to these benchmarks, the TV-PARX model's dynamic nature enables it to forecast counting time series data beyond the medium-term horizon more accurately. In contrast, the accuracy of forecasts converges for larger horizons in the cases studied. In summary, the time-varying Poisson AutoRegressive model with external covariates offers a valuable tool for counting time series data analysis, demonstrating its practical applications and forecasting capabilities across various scenarios and data sets. In particular, it provides medium-term forecasting performance gains, while the accuracy of its forecasts converges with increasing time in the cases examined. In the context of COVID-19 related research, the TV-PARX model can be used to forecast daily cases and deaths in different countries, while in corporate finance, it may be used to forecast defaulting firms among all public listings in a given stock market. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Notably, our analysis confirms the expected value of $\gamma$ to be approximately 1.47, 1.24 for $N=2, 4$ based on standard scaling theory. Furthermore, we have extended the investigation to include $N=1, 6$ universality classes in three dimensions and obtained corresponding results for these cases as well. Our study has implications for the scenario with a non-trivial critical point in QCD, suggesting that the approach to this critical point would be slow due to the relatively large distance between the Yang-Lee edge singularity and the transition temperature, making it challenging to detect. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality helped us to enumerate the possible states in the "hard" regime, as well as the corresponding probabilities, which correspond to the frozen and spin configurations in these models. Lastly, our inequality enabled us to determine the scalar and the dimensional factors that characterize the complexity of these configurations. These factors, which were previously unknown, will influence the dynamics of the Z2 synchronization problem and the knee distribution of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. The approach we used to establish our inequality combines the AMP algorithm with a specific variance reduction technique and both the matrix mean and the matrix square root of a particular co-contrast matrix. The resulting inequality shares some similarities with the existing covering lemma, but it extends the original conditions under which the covering lemma can be applied. The application of our inequality to the TAP free energy function specifically refers to the set of the complex configurations that the AMP algorithm can sample from, which is a direct result of the cut-message passing algorithm applied to a random intersection code. The information gained from this specific case also enabled us to analyze the knee distribution of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, which represents the densities of the spin configurations in the "hard" regime. Bouchaud ["Complexity and the knee distribution in random constraint satisfaction problems," Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical 46, no. 29 (2013): 295002]. The approach we used in this case first involved an analytical derivation of the knee distribution of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model based on the single-spin flip dynamics, which was then compared to the results obtained through the coverage inequality. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We further developed a new analytical approach to model the fractal scintillation patterns caused by the detectors' photon statistics, which are essential for accurately determining the system's non-linearity effects. By applying this research to previous and new observations, we successfully increased the precision of the aerosol depth measurements to 0.012 or less, meeting the required precision of 0.01. We also tested the stability of the system over time and found that regular calibration is necessary to maintain the desired precision, primarily due to gradual changes in the system's gain. By implementing this calibration, which involves analyzing raw data files directly, we can ensure the precision of the depth measurements remains consistently high across various observation periods. We also explored using other stellar targets and made adjustments to the analysis procedure accordingly. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a precision of 0.01 for the aerosol depth using photometry from stars within the U-band spectrum. We have made the software used in this research available for public use. The aerosol depth measurements we obtained from the combined FRAM and STA telescope datasets from 2015 to 2021 range from 0.1 to 0.3 and demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in monitoring atmospheric conditions over extended periods. The validity of these measurements was validated through comparisons with concurrent satellite data from MISR, OMI, and SUpeiRIAL, as well as other ground-based measurements from AERONET, which showed a consistent pattern of variability. The precision of these measurements has the potential to be further improved with the use of better CCD detectors, which could enhance the applicability of this method even further. The complete analysis procedure we developed is suitable for other similar telescopic systems that employ stellar photometry to measure the aerosol depth

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed code is now publicly available on the GitHub site www.github.com/XiaoningRan/ObjectPoseCode. Moreover, an interactive viewer for pose disassembly and reassembly can be found at www.objectpose.org. When applying the proposed framework to real-world applications, it is crucial to train the model on correspndences generated automatically by the PnP algorithm carefully, as our experiments showed that noisy correspondences may lead to poor performance. Therefore, we propose a simple yet effective approach to filter out unreliable correspondences based on the distance between 3D box center and corresponded 2D points, which is a more robust way of generating correspondences for training than the commonly used method of random correspondence generation. We also explored the relationship between pose prediction performance and the number of sampled correspondences, as well as the impact of adding our proposal to deep learning baselines using 2D-3D correspondences. Finally, we analyze the common failures of our network, such as predicting impossible poses or failing to detect objects, and provide suggestions on how to rectify these issues. We also compared our approach with a popular method using disk-based correspondences and presented a step-by-step object pose disassembly guide. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Overall, this most efficient method demonstrates significant potential for improving biomolecular simulations by leveraging the accuracy of numerical solutions to stochastic equations. Through further optimization, potential applications in other molecular simulations are also proposed. Through the public release of the code, the research encourages fellow scientists to contribute to the improvement of the algorithm. The code, titled TSTBVM, is now publicly accessible via GitHub, allowing for the seamless integration of the method into existing molecular dynamics software via an interface based on the CHARMM suite. In addition to TSTBVM, the research also provides a standalone platform called STSBVM-Tester, designed to facilitate the assessment and comparison of other numerical methods using the same standards and test cases. Both code packages are compatible with Linux operating systems. The research underlying the project was supported by the National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, and the computational resources provided by the Texas Advanced Computing Center. The public release of the code also marks the introduction of a novel performance evaluation framework for numerical methods in molecular dynamics simulations, which can be utilized by researchers and developers to compare and assess various methods using a standardized set of criteria. The code packages TSTBVM and STSBVM-Tester are available at https://github.com/Brownian-Motors/TSTBVM and https://github.com/Brownian-Motors/STSBVM-Tester, respectively. The related documentation can be found at https://brownian-motors.github.io

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness and simplicity of our approach by applying it to real-world data, including a case study of scientific collaboration networks. Additionally, our results show that our approach is comparable to other existing methods, including personalized Google Search, which can be seen as a variation of eigenvector centrality, and which achieves similar results with significantly reduced computational time. Our approach and associated code are available for public use. Our research provides a foundation for further exploration of eigenvector centrality in multi-layered networks, especially in the context of cross-layer community detection, where our approach has evident practical value. Our approach has already been utilized in a previous study published in the journal Chaos, which is a part of the same research agenda presented here. Our approach has been tested on real-world data, including a large Amazon product co-purchase network consisting of over 10 million connections across 150 million nodes in different layers, on which it demonstrated notable performance. Our research team believes that our approach and associated code will be useful to the scientific community worldwide. Our approach has been applied to a large financial network dataset containing over 1 million connections across 13 million nodes in different layers, on which it demonstrated significant performance. corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within

within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. By introducing the Dirac operator in the conformally flat 
de Sitter spacetime, we derive the explicit solutions for the wave function and energy 
levels. Furthermore, we analyze the energy spectrum and find that it obeys the universal 
scaling rule $\Delta E = \beta \hbar c^2$, where $\beta = 3.41$ holds true for all 
energy levels. We also determine the upper limit of energy levels and distinguish the 
criteria for classifying closed de Sitter spacetime. Lastly, we outline the relationship 
between the energy spectrum and the cosmological constant. We expect this study to serve 
as a starting point for investigating quantum fields in the Einstein static universe.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our extensive, high-speed visualization data also reveal the partial-seal stage's duration shortens as the speed of the falling sphere increases. Furthermore, our extensive analysis of the partial-seal stage, which was made possible by our high-speed visualization methods, provide the first detailed description of this stage, filling a significant knowledge gap in this area of fluid dynamics research. In the surface-seal regime, the relationship between the radius of the forming cavity and time is found to behave differently for low- and high-speed impact velocities. Ultimately, our study offers a comprehensive analysis of the water-entry interactions at mid-range speeds, filling a notable absence in previous research. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. The $\theta$-terms also produce a hierarchy of scales that can be used to explain the weakness of another fundamental force, an idea initially proposed by Witten, and which arises as an outcome of the monodromy transformation rather than a prior assumption. Furthermore, another boundary near which the moduli space could be established, and which is characterized by a different monodromy transformation, and which represents a different effective theory, is also contained within the range of the original effective theory. This leads to another force beyond gravity that cannot be considered weak within the context of the current effective theory, and which cannot be accounted for through the use of the standard alpha'-corrections. Instead, it arises from the monodromy transformation of the range of charged states, and which gives rise to a hierarchy of scales that can be parameterized by another quadratic gauge field strength and which is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, we find that cubanite's unique orbital behavior is attributed to the specific arrangement of its atoms, maintaining the individuality of both metallic and covalent states of the 3d electrons. This has implications for its electronic phase diagram, with potential pathways to novel states of matter such as heavy fermion or self-trapped electron behavior. Our study highlights the need for comprehensive theoretical understanding of cubanite's electronics and suggests that despite being a relatively stable compound, it can be driven towards novel mechanisms of superconductivity, ferromagnetism, or phase separation with potential applications. To this end, we propose simulations of cubanite under various conditions, with possible applications in materials science, physics, and chemistry. This work is a part of ongoing efforts to develop practical and theoretical frameworks for predicting the electronics of transition metal compounds with atomic arrangements similar to cubanite. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. This breakthrough poses an significant improvement over previous records of up to twenty-emitted phonons in one period, achieving a threshold of only three photons for emission, and reaching a conversion efficiency of 0.5% among the strongest reported so far. This finding also implies that even the most fragile dark states can be activated and may lead to a better comprehension of multi-phonon physics within the realm of dark matter. Moreover, researchers have observed unusual effects, including the generation of odd-numbered phonon bundles, the occurrence of double Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state, a dark exciton state, and a free carrier state, and the formation of a stationary dark-solitron-like state within the quantum dot coupled to the acoustic cavity. This discovery opens doors to novel applications and uncovers previously unknown phenomena in both physics and engineering disciplines. Additionally, this breakthrough suggests that even the most delicate dark states can be activated, potentially leading to a deeper understanding of complex physics within the 'dark matter' category. Furthermore, this finding demonstrates the potential for an acoustic phonon gun, which could serve as a model for developing similar devices based on other quantum fluctuations, such as magnetic or electrical noise. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Additionally, we outline the essential conditions for detecting these properties and the related experimental challenges. Moreover, we discuss the potential applications of SPCCSs in beyond-classical information processing and optical metrology. In the case of lossy devices, we develop a theoretical model to predict the non-classical behavior of SPCCSs, and our results are compared with experimental data obtained using a faulty beam splitter. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that the difficulty in maintaining zero temperature in experimental settings hinders the generation of truly coherent states in practical scenarios. Consequently, we propose a modified approach to achieve similar outcomes using a bistable device, such as a Sagnac interferometer, where the required temperature is more manageable. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive examination of SPCCSs, a novel and versatile class of quantum states that can be generated using simple linear optical devices, and sheds light on the importance of accurately defining success conditions to reveal their inherent non-classical behavior. This, in turn, can facilitate the development of various quantum technological applications. This research also offers a model for predicting the non-classical behavior of SPCCSs in the presence of losses, which can serve as a framework for experimenting with actual devices. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Our dataset is accessible upon request. Our model's potential limitations include its reliance on large datasets and memory-intensive computations. Our suggested approach has clinical implications by providing a more efficient, purely CT-based method for mapping tumors in the esophagus with acceptable accuracy. This is particularly significant in situations with limited resources or in trials evaluating novel agents or therapies. To foster progress in this area, we encourage other researchers to contribute their own esophageal CT scan datasets. Our model can be utilized for mapping other organs or tumors in the chest by modifying the input image dimensions. Our code and model are available online at https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Our dataset is accessible upon request. Our study was supported by the National Institutes of Health under grant number R01CA253469. Our institution also receives funding

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where people are more likely to hold firm beliefs, we observed increased dissemination of misinformation. These findings suggest that the spread of online misinformation is influenced by offline cultural patterns. We also discovered subgroups within Reddit that have been consistently exposed to misinformation over time, and that the most vulnerable populations could benefit from targeted misinformation correction campaigns. We propose a future direction for combating the spread of misinformation by incorporating the principles of mass communication and sociology into machine learning models. We have made the data and code for this study open for public use.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research paves the way for exploring ways to incorporate speech patterns into learning algorithms and robot control systems. Experimental data is available for download at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3QOE3Q. This work is an initial step towards understanding the auditory aspects of human instruction and it is hoped will spur further interest in exploring the auditory elements of human robot interaction. This study has several applications including developing more efficient learning algorithms, improving speech enabled robotic interfaces, enhancing robot manipulation via increased utilization of auditory feedback, and facilitating better understanding of the interplay between speech and action in human robot interaction. This knowledge can be utilized to enhance learning via demonstration, refine robot speech systems using self-supervised learning, prioritize auditory feedback for improved robot manipulation, and investigate the relationship between speech and action in human robot interaction via joint segmentation of audio and motion data. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose a approach that leverages a formal language to define desired system behavior, and employs a technique to compare the meaning of utterances. Furthermore, we present a method to determine whether a system satisfies a given specification, and provide an algorithm to accomplish this determination. This algorithm is underlined by a theory of equality between extended word meanings, and entails a metric that measures the similarity between these meanings. We have developed an prototype of our testing framework, and test it on a dummy system by presenting experimental data that highlights the limitations of the current implementation. We have also tested the equality theory and the algorithm on previously published test cases, and present the results of these experiments. Future research directions and potential challenges in this area are also discussed. This paper is an extended version of a technical paper that was previously presented at the Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, our further analysis reveals the practical applicability and feasibility of MSDCR in real-world settings. The code and datasets for this study are available at https://github.com/ChengLiUIBE/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Furthermore, Hypatia's versatility allows it to be used in conjunction with other solver engines via seamless integration with Julia's modeling APIs. The resulting data and methodology are thoroughly available for open scrutiny on GitHub and an associated technical report. The proposed method is consistently shown to yield better results when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations, using a diverse set of test cases and benchmark problems. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating robust, robust quality control pipelines into automated analysis workflows, but also stress the importance of reviewing and validating model generalizability on local datasets before deploying quality control systems at scale. This is particularly crucial for automated analysis of MRI data involving unique population characteristics. In addition, our research dataset frameworks are anticipated to facilitate future developments in MRIQC systems. Our findings and methodological assessments are anticipated to contribute to enhanced quality control methodologies for ongoing and future MRI research projects. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Our results reveal that private EVs can either enhance or decrease the time required for the grid to recover, depending on specific conditions, and highlight the potential benefits of implementing tailored transportation and energy policies. This research stems from a broader investigation into optimal management of transportation and energy networks in the presence of private EVs, with implications for grid resilience, and offers a foundation for exploring additional aspects, such as private EV adoption and grid management with private EVs, within both localized and broader scales. This research demonstrates the value of a unified transportation and energy framework that can be applied to various settings, prompting questions about the limitations of existing compartmentalized models. This involves considering additional variables, such as heat management, electric vehicle-to-grid technology, and private EV sharing services, and exploring policy recommendations that can be derived from this integrated perspective. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings show that this attractor exhibits sensitivity to parameter changes, resulting in the agents behaving in a random, seemingly chaotic manner. In the case study presented, we show that this behavior can be misunderstood as instability rather than chaos. In addition, our research reveals that the distribution of the agents' waiting times prior to meetings is exponentially distributed, supporting the conclusion that their dynamics are indeed chaotic in nature. In the process, we also address the critique that the original Motivation Dynamics model relies on an unrealistic assumption by illustrating that the model can accurately reflect real-world behavior if the time frame it operates within is viewed as infinitely large in comparison to the time scale of the agents' behavior. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our data suggest that the electronic and magnetic properties of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series are relatively stable across various Cm compositions, indicating they possess a wide range of possible engineering variations. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental properties of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, allowing for the prediction of their electronic and magnetic behavior in different Cm compositions. This knowledge can be utilized to design materials with desired performance levels for use in future spintronic devices. This research further highlights the potential of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series in tackling the challenge of scaling magnetic memory beyond the current limit of large-scale magnetic storage. This study's findings have been verified using the experimental data of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series obtained via X-ray diffraction and magnetization measurements. This research paves the way for theoretical prediction of the electronic and magnetic properties of layered intermetallic compounds in the AuCu3 structure type. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The model predicts the mass range of these composite particles to be around 0.5-50 TeV, and assumes that the actual mass of these particles will be within the reach of a future high-energy particle accelerator. The implied mass range of the individual heavy quarks is significantly larger, estimated to be in the order of a few TeV to tens of TeV. The model's predictions also involve the possibility of observing unique particles called "true" dark matter, which could have mass ranges compatible with current direct dark matter detection experiments, or masses beyond the reach of those experiments, potentially within the range of the LHC or a 100 TeV particle accelerator. The implied range of the composite dark matter particles is also vast, extending from the current direct dark matter detection experimental range to masses beyond the reach of the LHC or a 100 TeV particle accelerator. The paper concludes by reviewing the implied observation chances of the bilepton model's predictions with current and future particle accelerators and direct dark matter detection experiments. The paper also reviews the implied energy range of a particle accelerator required to detect the bilepton model's predicted physics phenomena with a 50% chance of observation. The implied energy range is found to be a 10 TeV particle accelerator for the observation of mass range compatible with the LHC and a 100 TeV particle accelerator for the observation of a significant portion of the predicted physics phenomena. The paper suggests that future high-energy particle accelerators are necessary to detect the implied physics phenomena of the bilepton model. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Ultimately, our investigation reveals that the standard ordered generating sequences comprise a generating set for the weak order on the subgroup Bn. What's more, we demonstrate that the Coxeter length of an element in Bn is equivalent to the sum of powers of corresponding standard generating sequence powers. Additionally, we establish that the descent set of Bn can be expressed in a form that is equivalent to the set of elements below a particular strong order, which we term the standard strong order. Finally, our research on the finite classical Coxeter group An reveals that the standard ordered generating sequences, weak order, Coxeter length, and descent set all behave identically to those of the group Bn. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this correction, we reanalyzed the Hubble diagram for SN Ia data from various observational sets, resulting in improvements in the constraint for the Hubble constant $H_0$ of up to $1.3\sigma$ in certain cases. Moreover, this approach enables the investigation of galactic halo properties from the characteristics of SN Ia events and other observational data. As such, this new method presents a valuable, broadly applicable technique with implications for the interpretation of future SN Ia data sets. To demonstrate this, we applied this approach to SN Ia supernovae within the JND dataset, typed as SNe Ia with narrow lines, and found that the characteristic density could serve as a lensing weight for these objects, allowing for the calculation of their mass and mass-to-light ratio. Finally, we propose that a similar method could be employed with deep fields of galaxy populations, which have been weakly lensed by galaxies selfsimilar at their centers. In this case, this approach could facilitate the investigation of the massdistribution of galaxies across various distances, as well as informing cosmological parameters based on future SN Ia generations, such as those from future surveys like LSST and JITP

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, this demonstration brings the quantum network's basic module, a waveguide integrated with a quantum bit, within reachable distances. Furthermore, we illustrate the capability to modify the fabrications conditions of the T center devices to trade off the 1550 nm wavelength sensitivity for higher T center densities, or vice versa. This versatility in device design will be crucial for addressing different quantum communication network applications. Ultimately, this research showcases the straightforward creation of efficient photon-spin interfaces using T center devices, positioned at the core of reliable and controlled quantum communication. Additionally, it is an early step towards developing a quantum communication device that incorporates a waveguide integrated with a quantum bit, tailored for real-world applications. Given the inherent compatibility with existing silicon photonic platforms, this approach also presents an opportunity to explore the integration of defect-based quantum bits with existing silicon photonic technologies. The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Furthermore, we have incorporated an extra term $\varepsilon h_i(x)$ into the system's equations, and demonstrated that this system shares the same solution set as the original system, when $\varepsilon$ tends towards zero. The approach introduced in this study can also be applied to a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic single equation. The study discussed in this paper provides an upgrade to the results that were achieved in a previous study on a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality, which enabled the solution of a specific problem that was raised in a previous research on a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. The underlying principles can be extended to a broader class of discrete probability distributions meeting certain conditions of uniformity, thereby yielding a range of pre-existing and new results for such distributions. The resulting generalised inequalities for uniform distributions can be used to derive new bounds for various problems, including those involving covering times of Markov chains, the mixing time of the lazy random walk, the concentration of polynomial functions on expander graphs, and the matrix-valued Schramm-Loewner dynamics. The current study offers a comprehensive framework combining, expanding, and refining upon earlier outcomes by the authors, as well as providing a unified source for the various inequalities derived, often through novel extensions, of the original research. The individual results from these earlier studies are: inequalities for convex functions and polynomial functions on the discrete cube, currently considered the most general possible; the Bernstein-type inequality for linear combinations of positive definite matrices; the widest possible bounds for subgaussian measures on the discrete cube; and the log-Sobolev inequalities, Talagrand's convex distance inequality, and the resulting consequences for random variables on the discrete cube. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Furthermore, conjugacy classes featuring non-trivial central characters are classified according to central characters, Hermitian forms, and quadratic forms. Conjugacy classes with a trivial central character are then characterized by specific combinations of polynomials and systems of integers. Failing that, these classes are categorized based on partial information obtained through the field of rational numbers, before ultimately deriving the distinctness of conjugacy classes via a deep analysis of symplectic Simon's Lemma and the properties of highly transitive groups. This research was initially published in the Journal of Algebra volumes 12 and 13. This version corrects minor changes to the original content. Additionally, two proofs previously given in the original publication have been removed, with an note on the Hermitian forms' equivalence class classification was also updated. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Additionally, we highlight ongoing developments, possible enhancements, and future opportunities, alongside the formal announcement of the `pdf4lhc` toolkit.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has helped in identifying novel genes associated with microsatellite expansion disorders and in distinguishing between different types of disorders linked to certain genomic variants such as SNPs related to type 1 and 2 diabetes primarily targeting different cellular environments. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The observed pattern of recurrence times also aligns with a power-law distribution, with specific parameters that factor in detection limitations, and is unaffected by the presence of black holes among the binary population. The study further suggests that the majority of the stellar mass binary population is composed of non-accretors, featuring a power-law distribution from 1 to 10 million years, and the search for a correlation between recurrence times and specific orbital periods or pulsar spin periods was unsuccessful. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. This approach has been made available for public use on GitHub at the time of writing. Furthermore, this paper identifies instances in which Diversity Threshold Generation excels over existing methods, such as Improved Sequence Generation through Global Inference, Multiple Sentence Ordering, and Dialog Diversity Enhancement via Priority-Setting Agents. In addition, it offers potential areas for future research, including incorporating additional factors such as tone and tone-aware Diversity Threshold Generation. This study was conducted in conjunction with the WNGTNLP 2021 conference and is based on a previous paper presented at the EMNLP 2021 conference. In both instances, the underlying data was a convolutional dialog dataset called ConvAI2, which consisted of 5,000 human-conducted conversations between humans and a retort-generating model known as Bob. This data was utilized to test the proposed metric, which revealed a clear connection between NLI Diversity and semantic variety, as well as the effectiveness of Diversity Threshold Generation, which was found to result in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity over existing methods. Finally, this paper acknowledges the limitations of the current state of NLI Diversity, which are discussed in the conclusion section. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In addition, an algorithm has been created to find the minimum number of nodes necessary to break in order to obtain a planar representation, and this number can serve as a threshold to evaluate the ease of visualizing a given bipartite graph. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach is viable for large-scale graphs. The approach has been applied to investigate various bipartite graphs characterized by their internal and between-group connection patterns, and to analyze the relationship between these patterns and the difficulty of visualizing their structure. In the process, a novel metric has been introduced to quantify the ease of visualizing such structures, and it has been found that this ease is unaffected by the speed at which new connections between existing pairs of entities form, but it is affected when the option of forming such connections is available. In the same context, an investigation has been carried out to determine the conditions under which a random graph with a specific structure can be easily visualized. In addition, the relationship between the distribution of connections within the groups and the ease of visualizing their bipartite graph has been examined, and it has been found that this ease increases more slowly than any power of the number of connections existing within the groups, but it increases faster than any power of minus the proportion of such connections, and it remains unchanged when the form of these connections follows a specific distribution. In the same area of research, an analysis has been conducted to explore the relationship between another form of connections distribution and the ease of visualizing a bipartite graph. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Notably, our method is found to consistently outperform RFF, often to a significant degree, and also compares favourably to orthogonal random features and the Nyström method in various scenarios. In addition to its scalable kernel approximation capabilities, this method can be configured to efficiently utilize meta-information, thereby enabling the construction of graph-structured random features that accurately reflect underlying data relationships. We rigorously examine the theoretical properties of this method and demonstrate its practical advantages through comprehensive experimental evaluations conducted across a broad range of applications and datasets. In summary, this paper presents an innovative solution to kernel approximation that surpasses existing methods, simplifies the incorporation of meta-information, and empowers the scalable application of kernel methods to complex, real-world datasets. We make the code and models available for public use at https://github.com/yin1016/efficient-kernel approximation. Nevertheless, this metric has its limitations, particularly when comparing models for different datasets. In such cases, a more suitable comparison would be based on the number of model parameters versus the achieved accuracy, rather than a plain accuracy assessment. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a meta-learning framework that enables the comparison of models for different datasets based on their parameter efficiency. We test and evaluate this framework using two examples: (1) comparing the efficiency of different model architectures on a single dataset, and (2) comparing the efficiency of models on multiple datasets with varying characteristics. In both instances, our results show that our proposed method produces more accurate comparisons than conventional methods.
