This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. If this hypersurface is not compact, we found that it can be mapped to a compact hypersurface with the mentioned topology for values of r less than 1, specifically when r is equal to the square root of 1 plus the reciprocal of the square root of 1. If this hypersurface is compact with this specific value of r, we are able to calculate its total surface area. Additionally, we examined and reported the results of testing this area against the expected value based on its topological properties, discovering that it matches the predicted value exactly. Moreover, we studied and defined the term "positive scalar curvature" for this type of hypersurface, discovering that it does not exist. Lastly, we studied and analyzed the relationship between this hypersurface's scalar curvature and its radius, discovering that the relationship is constant and specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1, causing it to be constantly negatively curved except in a singular point. This research was inspired by the works of G.M. Ewing and S. Yau. It was also influenced by the hypersurface research conducted by the authors themselves. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, threshold values are established to determine when the removal of an individual node leads to the main component breaking into two or more distinct components. Additionally, the average size of the removed component is calculated and analyzed in depth. Interestingly, an intriguing non-monotonic pattern is observed in this calculation. In addition, the removal of a single node that results in the main component splitting into two or more components is also analyzed. Finally, this paper also considers the case where the maximum allowed distance between nodes can limit the removal of nodes from the main component. In this scenario, lower and upper bounds are established to determine the average size of the removed component. Notably, these bounds differ by more than one unit, highlighting the complexity of this problem. Despite the appeal of this research, there are some difficult mathematical problems that need to be resolved. To overcome these challenges, this paper is a starting point for future research on simpler network models, such as regular networks and small world networks. Consequently, the intricate analysis provided in this paper can be used as a reference for similar research on these more complex networks. Ultimately, this paper aims to initiate a novel approach to understanding network vulnerability by examining the effects of removing individual nodes on a large scale. By applying mathematical theories to network analysis, new research questions are raised that are relevant to various networks. Therefore, this paper can serve as a precursor to future research on more sophisticated networks. Moreover, the Cayley tree network serves as a fundamental model that can be used to investigate general network principles and patterns. By exploring the complex relationships between node removal sizes and network structures, this paper can serve as a foundation for investigating non-normal distribution patterns of node removal sizes. In addition, the explicit expressions derived in this paper can provide valuable insights into network component splitting and breaking.

We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. We found that this gate design offers the optimal balance of motion-based entanglement loss and frequency-based entanglement loss among all possible designs, outperforming conventional Molmer-Sorensen gates by exceeding a twenty-fold improvement in frequency robustness while maintaining comparable precision for short chains of ions. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves realistic results when applied to synthetic datasets generated from 3D face models. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the inherent challenges in altering a unit's risk tolerance, our recommendation is to focus on developing risk-affordable storage technology to ensure these systems operate in the best interest of their owners, even if it means forgoing some potential earnings. This approach is expected to lead to healthier financial outcomes and more valuable storage units in the long run. Furthermore, our results provide a risk-affordable storage unit assessment tool that market operators and regulators can utilize to evaluate the suitability of storage units participating in certain markets. This is particularly important for ensuring fair market access for all storage units, given the differences in risk preferences currently leading to exclusion from certain markets. This approach can also be applied to other electricity markets around the world. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. All experiments were conducted at very low temperatures using a vector magnetic field, and the results were confirmed through measurements of the Hall effect. Notably, the resistance of the most sensitive samples was extremely high, reaching values in the order of megagaus, and was found to be insensitive to both the direction of the vector magnetic field and its intensity. This behavior is exceptional among semiconductors. A notable feature of the resistance peaks was their extremely long duration, which could be primarily attributed to the very slow movement of the ferromagnetic edge channels. This phenomenon was found to occur throughout the range of HgTe quantum well sizes examined, and is believed to be a fundamental property of the material. A hypothetical proposal has been put forward to utilize the unique properties of HgTe quantum wells to create magnetic field-regulated, high-resistance switches. This concept is based on the neutral edge state's robustness in the neutral point of the samples, and the extremely long edge channel relaxation time. This could potentially enable the development of magnetic field-controlled, large gap semiconductors with very high resistance levels. This idea has been referred to as "Magnetic Regulated Gap Engineering" (MARGE). In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Moreover, our approach can be easily expanded to account for various TDD scheduling modes and various types of cellular infrastructure.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our proposed system demonstrates comparable performance to models trained on larger datasets, as seen in comparisons with current robust machine learning methods. We also introduce a new reliability metric, called the distance metric, which provides a quantitative measure of a model's reliability and serves as a benchmark for evaluating future robust machine learning techniques. We make the code and datasets available for public use.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, the study validates the integrity of developed models utilizing an out-of-domain WSD data set, demonstrating their robustness and reliability.  The proposed framework and augmentation techniques exhibit potential for expanding WSD beyond its current limitations by integrating other knowledge bases and exploring different context-gloss augmentation strategies.  The code and models associated with this study are available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/zhuyonghui/WordSenseAug.  Further research is necessary to address issues related to data augmentation over-saturation and the potential negative impact of context-gloss augmentation on precise sense identification in WSD.  Nonetheless, this study demonstrates the feasibility and efficacy of integrating WSD with data augmentation techniques that incorporate lexical knowledge bases, paving the way for the development of more efficient and more knowledgeable WSD models.  The associated data sets, models, and experimental results can be found at this link https://github.com/zhuyonghui/WordSenseAug. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the phase space distribution of the top quark was found to conform to quantum chromodynamics predictions, with measurements for individual kinematic characteristics, such as the transverse momentum and longitudinal momentum of the top quark, and the number of subjet pairs within jet cones, also aligning with predicted values. The research also yielded measurements for single top quark production, at levels of 8 nanobarns with a 12-nanobarn uncertainty in the proton-lead collision environment. The findings expand upon previous experiments conducted using antiproton-proton collisions. The research is also significant in providing reference values for single and pair-produced top quark decays in heavy ion collisions. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Additionally, this approach extends previous hydrodynamic descriptions, enabling the simulation of interacting Bose gas dynamics in optimal averaging schemes, which were previously limited to equilibrium situations. This new method demonstrates its effectiveness by accurately replicating existing hydrodynamic results and showing its potential in modeling intricate dynamics of quantum systems at the interface of quantum and classical behaviors. This novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach offers a significant advancement in the dynamical theory of interacting Bose gases, and its simplicity makes it an attractive solution for integrating quantum dynamics into classical simulations of entire systems and experiments. This development is particularly significant for optimal averaging schemes, which are now capable of simulating entire non-equilibrium trajectories of quantum systems at the same level of accuracy as local quantum properties. This research paves the way for further exploration of the interplay between quantum behaviors and external perturbations in finite systems, and it also leads to an improved understanding of the limitations of existing hydrodynamic theories, particularly in regards to the validity of linearized descriptions within shock wave scenarios. This new method is readily applicable to a broad range of experimental setups, including the study of interacting Bose gases in optical lattices, especially in scenarios involving sudden changes of external conditions. This development is also relevant to closed systems, where it allows for the accurate simulation of full quantum trajectories even in the presence of broken symmetries, and it demonstrates the importance of considering the full quantum dynamics when studying the dynamics of interacting Bose gases, especially in non-equilibrium situations. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, we've made the paired-permutation test exact in the large dataset limit, meaning our algorithm can be fast and accurate for large datasets without a substantial increase in computational time. We've also introduced a new metric, the exact paired-permutation test time (EPTT), to standardize assessments of the algorithm's performance. Finally, we've made the paired-permutation test exact in the large dataset limit available to the community through an easy-to-use Python package called permtest Exact results are crucial in ensuring the integrity of statistical tests, and our efforts are intended to promote the use of reliable test methods throughout the field of NLP. We hope this contribution accelerates the adoption of exact paired-permutation tests among practitioners and researchers worldwide. We've publicly released the code and guidelines for evaluating the EPTT at https://github.com/lincoln-h/permtest-fast. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, it is shown that each loom space can be characterized by a specific kind of veering triangulation, with this characterization being inherently distinct from its definition as a leaf space. Furthermore, it is proven that the volume of the veering triangulation is essentially zero. A notable consequence arises from the fact that veering triangulations are topologically equivalent to 3D space, leading to the conclusion that they do not support a meaningful notion of volume. Nonetheless, it is possible to define the volume of a veering triangulation as the volume of its associated loom space. It is then demonstrated that this defined volume is essentially zero for all veering triangulations. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This approach allowed us to estimate the drag experienced by the cylinder in both orientations and how it changed with speed and the fraction of anisotropy. This knowledge could be valuable in understanding how sedimentation affects plants and animals. This approach also involved developing a method for estimating the drag experienced by a flat end by comparing the drag experienced by a circular shape with that of a square one. This approach further involved verifying that the drag experienced by a solid moving through a liquid behaved differently than it did in a granular material. This difference in behavior was found to be due to the limited anisotropy of drag experienced by a solid in a liquid, which was very small indeed. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Furthermore, our findings also revealed that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow increases with centrality, which we attribute to initial collision configuration's growing influence in more central collisions. Moreover, our research demonstrated that triangular flow can be accurately described by a simple ratio formula based on elliptical flow and average number of participants. Our results are viewable in the form of figures within the paper. Our investigations provide a deeper understanding of triangular flow's dynamics and offer a usable tool for identifying triangular flow in future experiments. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. Specifically, researchers have made the following discoveries with a 2019 dataset of 3.0 inverse picobarns of proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy: - The measured rate of $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ events falls within the expected parameter range defined by the CKM theory, with an estimated uncertainty of 0.02. - The most precise evaluations to date of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ decay, yielding results that also align with the CKM theory and featuring an improved uncertainty of 0.06. - The most accurate assessments of rare $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ events also have been achieved, with results consistent with theoretical models incorporating the CKM theory and an estimated precision of 2.38*10^-5. These significant advancements in the understanding of neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, facilitated by a substantial enhancement in processing power and a marked decrease in data acquisition costs, pave the way for future discoveries in this field, given the potential of the LHC for producing large numbers of rare B-meson decays. With increased dataset availability, particularly that expected from the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, researchers anticipate substantial improvements in the precision of these measurements. In fact, with 300 inverse picobarns of data at a 13 TeV energy, the ATLAS experiment is poised to enhance the precision of $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ measurements by factors of 3 and 5 respectively, and further advance the understanding of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ decay. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is shown to be viable for both explicit and implicit time-stepping methods, and its effectiveness is illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. The results show that by combining the modified flexible generalised minimum residual iteration with the spectral element method, both property preservation and high accuracy can be achieved, even in the presence of complex geometric configurations. The study's contributions are demonstrated by applying the proposed method to the minimax problem, a model often used to test numerical methods due to its complex behaviour, and compares it against existing schemes using different time-stepping methods. The results show that the proposed method achieves a higher accuracy while preserving the same property preservation properties of the original solution, especially when solving the 2D and 3D minimax problems using the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation model. The study also provides the code for the modified flexible generalised minimum residual iteration scheme, known as Theta-Smith CGI, which is compatible with major numerical software platforms. The code has been designed to be highly configurable, allowing users to easily change the underlying time-stepping method, numerical scheme, and problem parameters by modifying simple text files. The study recommends the theta method as the time-stepping scheme of choice for preserving property preservation properties, and suggests that the use of 20-30 time steps for each spatial refinement provides the best balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The study's results also highlight the importance of using appropriate iteration tolerance settings to avoid disrupting property preservation preservation, and suggests that higher tolerance settings can be used while still preserving the original solution's properties. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. Furthermore, we present a straightforward approach to incorporate external information, such as intraoperative contrast agent mapping, into the registration process. The resulting navigation data can be utilized for further analytical purposes, such as estimating blood distribution in the liver. The development of an efficient non-rigid registration algorithm for soft-tissue navigation in laparoscopic liver surgery makes the procedure more accurate and allows for additional analytical applications. Also, the code is publicly available online. It can be found at: https://github.com/Chen-2019-NRISNR. The evaluation data can be found at: https://github.com/Chen-2019-NRISNR-data. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We hope this dataset and proposed method will serve as a foundation for future research efforts. Code and dataset are available at: \url{https://github.com/Yueqing Liu/SceneFlowBenchmark}.

Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. This proposed algorithm leverages the benefits of both random neural networks and spiking neural networks, demonstrating its potential as a promising classifying model. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. By utilizing the equation of state, we studied spin-polarized strange quark star cores and computed the specific heat capacity, susceptibility, and other relevant thermodynamic properties. Conversely, we determined the maximum allowed temperature and spin polarization for quark stars in models with and without a neutron star companion. Lastly, we calculated the cooling layers and the lifetime of quark stars. Notably, for certain parameters, we found spin-polarized strange quark star masses that agree with observational data, and we also determined the relationships between the quark star mass and both temperature and spin polarization. Ultimately, our findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the physical properties and possible observations of spin-polarized strange quark stars. The research mentioned above leads to a comprehensive understanding of spin-polarized strange quark stars, facilitating future observations. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the PMH-property is not necessary for the E2F condition in cubic graphs, albeit without providing a constructive example. Instead, we offer a non-constructive proof by utilizing a infinite set of E2F cubic graphs that arise from an uncountable number of possible structures. Our research also involves introducing the super-edgetic operator, which can generate an infinite number of distinct E2F cubic graphs from a single base graph meeting specific criteria. Moreover, we examine the relationship between the prime number $p$ and the associated E2F cubic graph resulting from the operator, discovering that the graph corresponds to the field $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ if $p$ is a prime number, or the field $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ with an indeterminate embedded within its structure if $p$ is not a prime number. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Ultimately, Timeloops' advantages make it an appealing alternative for implementing static analysis-based techniques in important domains like cloud computing. The source code for Timeloops is available at https://timeloops.cs.purdue.edu/.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets. Experimental results confirm the advantage of using grid-based representations and the efficacy of the proposed algorithm. Furthermore, target density grids can be made accessible for visualization purposes. A key advantage of this filter variation is its relatively modest computational demand. Experiments conducted used various target densities and sensor configurations demonstrated the approach's versatility. A major application of this research is in the context of infrared sensor systems used for battlefield surveillance. Experimental data used in testing the algorithm was obtained from real-world infrared sensor systems. A key limitation of the algorithm is its initial requirement for a precise estimation of target density, which serves as its starting point. Nevertheless, the method presents a promising solution for estimating target densities in battlefield applications. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the probe size is more 
sensitive to the fill-factor than other design attributes. Consequently, our optimal 
'full-pattern' design is recommended for template-based imaging and spectroscopy 
in uncorrected TEMs. Moreover, we explore the feasibility of producing the proposed 
phase plates using current fabrication technologies, with estimated production times 
and costs. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the versatility of programmable 
phase plates in addressing various image quality challenges faced by TEM users. 
Given the fixed nature of traditional phase plates, users must either forgo using 
high-resolution capabilities or never utilize the probe fully, whereas programmable 
phase plates can accommodate changing probe requirements in real-time, without 
sacrificing resolution. In practice, this means that users can switch freely 
between low- and high-resolution imaging, without the need for time-consuming 
alignments, by simply changing the phase plate's programming, rather than physically 
replacing the traditional phase plate. In effect, a programmable phase plate 
enjoys the benefits of multiple traditional phase plates, with different fill-factors 
and pixel patterns available at the user's discretion, without the necessity of 
physical plate exchanges. Consequently, the term 'programmable phase plate' is henceforth 
referred to as 'PPPs in sequence' to avoid confusion. Notably, our proposed designs 
exceed the performance of current traditional phase plates by 20-30% in terms of 
probe size. Given the established benefits of programmable phase plates, including 
their ability to adjust probe sizes in sequence, our research provides a scientific 
foundation for the widespread adoption of PPPPs in TEM applications. In addition, 
our studies reveal possible fabrication challenges

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our research reveals the individual
migration histories of approximately 500 nuclei spanning multiple IKNM cycles, allowing us to explore the role of
retinal IKNM on the spatial distribution of neurons within the retina. We also leverage our data to evaluate previous
retinal IKNM modeling approaches and propose a more accurate model to predict the precise migration paths of new
nuclei and ultimately gain a deeper understanding of the interkinetic nuclear migration dynamics that underlie retinal
development. Our study demonstrates the value of using high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging techniques
in combination with precise modeling to gain a richer understanding of the complex cellular behaviors observed
during neural development. The interkinetic nuclear migration data, models, and software used in this research are
available for further utilization and building upon. The need for non-uniform cell randomization within the retina is
demonstrated, and the retina development dataset provides a foundation for exploring other aspects of neural development,
including cell fate selection and the formation of retinal layers. The methodology employed in this study can be
applied to the analysis of neural development in other systems and organisms. The zebrafish retina IKNM dataset is
accessible through the following links: https://github.com/mbegstrup/retina-developmental-imaging and
https://doi.org/10.34861/20241230180001. The software used for data analysis and modeling is available at the following
link: https://github.com

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments.  ReCross's simplicity, efficiency, and excellent performance make it a compelling choice for unlocking the full potential of massive language models across various tasks.  Our code is available at https://github.com/leimengzhen/recross.  Our findings also reveal that models with stronger capabilities tend to benefit more greatly from ReCross, and the method's effectiveness extends to both single-model and ensemble settings, offering considerable ensemble benefits with minimal additional cost.  Ultimately, our research demonstrates significant gains from ReCross in tasks like superglue, with improvements of up to 13 points in F1-score.  We propose ReCross as a fundamental technique for uncovering the underlying cross-task generalization abilities of massive language models. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Furthermore, we establish connections between the boolean complex and existing literature on subspaces of reflections in Coxeter groups, also exploring properties of these subspaces. Specifically, for the symmetric group S_n, we find that the boolean complex corresponds to the set of imbeddings of the braid axis A_n into the group's permutation representation on the vector space C, leading to a calculation of the number of spheres as C^(n-1) - 1. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between the boolean complex and its interaction with the screen partial order. Lastly, we observe that the homotopy type of the boolean complex also represents the screen partial order's poset of levels. By combining this observation with previous results, we conclude that the homotopy type of the boolean complex can be realized as a cascade of spheres, with each sphere in a level of the partial order being linked to the spheres in the subsequent level by means of a connection as described by a tube of dimension 2. This representation prompts an examination of the boolean complex's connection to the Coxeter group's geometry, especially in relation to its line segment, generating set dynamics, and the associated random walk. Consequently, we discover conditions guaranteeing that the line segment contains a specific point within the group, leading to an extension of the previous results for the finite Coxeter groups, notably including the groups Sn and Bn. Finally, we conclude by highlighting some potential applications of our research, including connections to branching processes, genus distribution, and the group's generation by random walk. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Finally, we conducted an policy-based experiment using the ROMI framework, suggesting that targeting the medium of propagation, promoting vaccine adoption, and releasing accurate health information could be effective strategies for governing the spread of rumors. Additionally, our research revealed that the influence of a rumor is limited to 3.59 days, indicating that timely intervention is crucial. To facilitate further research, we have made the data and proposed model available for public access. To address the diffusion problems caused by harmful online rumors, we propose integrating the ROMI framework with multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, yielding optimized policy results. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. Moreover, a significant agreement was observed between the planetary nebulae-based and previously estimated masses of the galaxies. A significant discovery has been made regarding the line-of-sight velocity dispersion of the galaxies within the Fornax cluster, specifically that there is a direct proportionality between this dispersion and the planetary nebulae-based mass of each galaxy. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. The advantages of LifeStream are further highlighted by its ability to efficiently process incremental computations, thus minimizing the overhead associated with data base updates. To facilitate widespread adoption, LifeStream is accompanied by a comprehensive benchmark, along with a user-friendly command-line interface and GUI tools for physician interaction. The code and benchmark are available at \url{https://lstream.io}.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we propose a novel approach called Neural Network Loss Explorer (NLLuxe), an iterative process that addresses this question by treating the loss function itself as a feature to be classified. NLLuxe surpasses results achieved with static loss functions on validation data sets commonly used to evaluate deep learning techniques, highlighting the potential to expand its impact through tailored implementations taking into account problem-specific characteristics, data sets, and other factors that influence classification performance. Our research, along with the related code and models, is available for public access at https://github.com/Qianhewu/NLLuxe.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. Computational examples demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed model and its efficiency in predicting material crystallization, shear band formation, and temperature changes during loading. The proposed model has been evaluated using experimental data from tension tests of polypropylene samples, which show a high degree of accuracy in predicting mechanical and thermal properties even in the presence of material failure. The accuracy and efficiency of this model make it a valuable tool for the simulation of polymer crystallization during production processes and product application testing. The proposed model has been made available for public use through the open source Limodin platform following the FAIR data principles. The model's limitations are also addressed in the research, along with strategic recommendations for its improvement. The research paper is accompanied by an animated video illustrating the simulated shear band formation and temperature changes in polypropylene samples during tension tests. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. A necessary condition for spin-triplet nematic superconductivity to occur in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also determined to be a relatively small electron concentration. A discussion of the limitations of the Ginzburg-Landau approach and the need for further investigation into the bulk properties of the material are also addressed. A proposal for investigating the magnetic susceptibility of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ through the use of a torque magnetometer is also presented. A summary of the main results is also provided in the form of a mean field theory analysis. A analysis of the stability of the chiral phase in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also provided. A discussion of the relevance of electron-electron interaction to the material Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also presented. A review of existing experimental and theoretical research on the material Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also presented. A discussion of the possible effects of sample inhomogeneity on the results of experiments is also addressed. A possible way to investigate the inhomogeneity of samples is also proposed. A review of the possible mechanisms of superconductivity in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also provided. A proposal for investigating the pairing function of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also presented. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. The proposed method enhances the performance of conventional differential detection, yielding higher signal-to-noise ratios by up to $6.8$ dB for certain CPM formats. The advantage of using $K$-symbol delays is further demonstrated to extend beyond ideal channel conditions, making this method's applications versatile. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our proposed approach provides a foundation for incorporating inferential knowledge into artificial intelligence models and offers a potential solution to the challenge of scaling such models through transfer learning following an initial training phase. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. NISQ-HHL's compact scale makes it suitable for desktop computation. The paper further presents a previously unseen, scalable methodology for calculating the number of qubits necessary for executable phase estimation and presents numerical results for a variety of scenarios involving real-world datasets and benchmark problems. These outcomes demonstrate the feasibility of employing the HHL using Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware for a variety of applications, including the optimization of small-scale portfolios, chemical reaction rate prediction, and protein-ligand binding affinity estimation. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This confirms the effectiveness of the proposed attention mechanism in efficient ASR using multi-modal learning. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. This method allows us to apply existing findings, initially presented by Berman and Aldous, which pertain to the asymptotic behavior of the first $k_n$ random walk steps. This approach also enables the extension of existing limit theorems for random walk steps to their equivalent formulations. The results we obtained in this study can be viewed as parking-specific interpretations of the findings initially presented by Berman and Aldous. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The discovery of this universal periodic shift of $2.84k_B T/J_c0$ may also be relevant to understanding the decay of $J_c0$ with temperature. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In order to facilitate integration with existing research on this topic, we also present results in a format compatible with widely used modeling frameworks, and highlight the limitations of our current research that provide a foundation for future work. Our study demonstrates that the 'well mixed' model often assumed in modeling the spread of airborne diseases may not always be accurate, and thus requires careful validation before it can be trusted. In the case of our analysis of a bus, we found that it significantly overestimates the distance that aerosol particles can travel through the air, with consequences for predictions of the risk of airborne transmission. In order to improve these predictions, we recommend that future research incorporates more realistic models of the dynamic interaction between people, airflow, and aerosol particles. In addition, we propose that the term 'well mixed' be used with caution in the context of airborne transmission, and that the conditions under which it is valid be clearly defined in each individual study. In the appendix, we provide detailed information about the bus geometry used in our analysis, as well as the parameters of the model used to simulate the formation and dispersal of aerosol particles. Moreover, we demonstrate the importance of properly modeling the distribution of aerosol particles when evaluating the effectiveness of different ventilation strategies in reducing transmission risk. Finally, we outline the potential applications and extensions of our model, and highlight the importance of considering the effects of surface deposition of aerosol particles on the prediction of transmission risk. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, a model based on the elastic scattering hypothesis successfully explains the magnetic anisotropy and Hall effect phenomena observed in the multilayer structure. Moreover, the magnitude of the Anomaltous Hall Resisitivity remains consistent across all Cobalt layer thickness levels, indicating that the spin-orbit proximity effect leads to a level of ferromagnetism persistence in the most outer Cobalt layers. This study demonstrates that elastic scattering of free carriers by the interface sites at which the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect occurs can result in unusual physical properties in bulk layers during multilayer construction. Hence, the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect's wider impact on physical properties in layered structures offers a significant level of controllability. A natural extension of this research involves investigating the effects of strong spin-orbit materials on hollow nanowires and nanotubes. The discovery presented here may also be integrated into Josephson junctions made from hybrid superconductor/ferromagnet materials. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We hope the underlying research will serve as a foundation for further development of methods that focus on input sensitivity, such as the development of neural networks that are invariant to camera angle, as indicated by our initial results. We have made the code and data for our experiments publicly available. The code can be found at https://github.com/ruishewang/LipNN and the data at https://github.com/ruishewang/Datasets.
