Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Furthermore, this framework demonstrates improved performance in a multi-center study involving 15 subjects from different populations and backgrounds. Additionally, the code and models are available for public use.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. Nonetheless, the study concludes that the primary driver of connections within the text is the relationship between successive statements themselves, with the underlying ideas of CT still valuable for understanding this coherence. However, the study also suggests that the underlying ideas of CT are not sufficient to capture the connections within the text and that researchers need a more comprehensive model that incorporates additional aspects. This revised CT can be utilized as a benchmark for assessing computer systems that identify connections within the text. Moreover, the study reveals that the relationship between successive statements is influenced by the system's knowledge and its tendency to favor more recent statements, providing insights that may guide the development of these computer systems. This study contributes to the field of natural language processing by utilizing a complex analysis that yields actionable information, unlike previous studies that relied on intuitive judgments. This paper focuses on search-based computer systems that identify connections within the text, but the underlying ideas of CT itself has been widely accepted and forms the basis of many other analyses. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Additionally, this research reveals that typically used linear threshold current ratios underestimate actual requirements by 2-4, implying that current standards tend to conserve capabilities of particle accelerators. Furthermore, an empirical formula derived from this study can be used to improve existing linear threshold current standards, allowing for more efficient use of energy recovery linacs. Experimental verification of theoretical and numerical results is also presented either directly from own research or by referencing established studies in the field. The findings presented in this research can be useful for designing and optimizing future energy recovery linacs, especially those with multi-pass designs. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. By contrast, under the NMRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV resists such decomposition, thereby demonstrating a more intricate structure that reflects both color and kinematic dependencies. In the limit of ultra-large rapidity spacing, the BFKL equation at NNLL accuracy requires knowledge of the one-loop six-gluon amplitude in all possible collinear configurations, encompassing not just the one-loop two-gluon CEV but also higher-order corrections to the BFKL gap survival factor, comprising collinear emissions in both dispersive and adjoint channels. Although the one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory exhibits a complex, NMRK-ordered structure in both color and kinematic dependencies, it can be represented using a minimal set of underlying components, namely the one-loop two-gluon CEV, a one-loop three-gluon CEV, a one-loop four-gluon impact factor, a one-loop quark-antiquark gap jet, and a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in a collinear configuration. These components, in turn, can be combined to derive higher-order corrections to the BFKL gap survival factor, thereby illustrating the central importance of the one-loop two-gluon CEV within the broader context of the BFKL equation. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Furthermore, this study provides a useful framework for incorporating curved brush geometries into coexistence curve calculations, phase field models, and other multi-scale simulations. Overall, this research demonstrates that the strengths and limitations of highly elongated brushes can be tailored through the selection of surface curvature. The developed theory also reveals the intricate relationships between brush geometry, free energy, and chain end distribution in curved surfaces, revealing the fundamental reasons behind the challenges of predicting the microstructure of block copolymer melts. This knowledge can be utilized to improve the predictive capabilities of coexistence curve calculations and phase field models. This study's findings are expected to contribute significantly to the understanding and simulation of block copolymer melt microstructure, with implications for the development of scalable simulations. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We determine the value of beta_k for graphs that look like a line (path) and a cycle (ring) and show it can be either k-1 or k when the graph is any other shape, depending on whether it's possible to travel between any two points in up to k steps. We also examine how changing the maximum distance affects the metric dimension of these other graphs. Finally, we discuss some possible variations of this new property. This new idea can be applied to three-dimensional versions of graph shapes known as 3D meshed networks. We offer some possible real-world applications of this new concept. This research was motivated by a problem in quantum computing known as the "quantum metric dimension problem". We provide a straightforward approach to determine the beta_k of any graph shape. We recognize that this approach is very similar to the way the metric dimension of a graph is calculated, but we choose to use a different name for it metric dimension to see if it sheds some light on the quantum metric dimension problem. We propose using the term "quantum distance" to describe the number of qubit measurements needed to pinpoint a specific qubit in a quantum computer. We define a new concept called the "quantum distance" of a network, which is similar to the "metric dimension" of a network, however it takes into account the physical constraints of a quantum computer. We explore the relationship between the quantum distance of a network and the number of qubit measurements required to pinpoint a specific qubit in a quantum computer. We propose an algorithm to determine the quantum distance of a network, which is equivalent to the metric dimension of a network, however it considers the maximum number of qubit measurements within a specific time frame, rather than considering all possible measurements. We refer to this new concept as beta_k of the network. We apply this new concept to solve the quantum metric dimension problem for linear, cyclic networks, as well as more complex networks, by examining how changing the maximum number of qubit measurements affects the quantum distance of these networks. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Despite the need for regular retraining to account for seasonal changes in source brightness, this method offers a robust approach to enhancing astronomical image analysis. Furthermore, the detailed representation of image structures provides a strong foundation for source extraction and allows for the assessment of analysis results and the inclusion of additional machine learning capabilities, such as object classification. This work leverages an significant amount of data and presents results that can be applied to current space telescopes, including the Fermi, Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, and the Telescope Array. Furthermore, the code developed as part of this research is openly available, enabling the machine learning-based analysis of future high-energy sky surveys, such as the Square Kilometre Array. By incorporating multiple representations of images and source extraction algorithms, this research enables the fair comparison of different machine learning-based analysis methods and algorithms. Furthermore, it provides a framework for addressing the limitations of current approaches, such as managing seasonally varying sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. This research is relevant to various current and future space telescopes, including the Fermi, Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, the Telescope Array, and the Square Kilometre Array. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We also introduce an associated variation, the conditional price of serial dictatorship, that takes into account the value of each action for agents. We test and analyze these metrics across various optimization domains and query settings, obtaining interesting results that favor solutions with lower price of serial dictatorship. We further investigate methods to reduce the price of serial dictatorship through the addition of fair payment schemes and agent feedback, discovering that these techniques are equally effective in enhancing the quality of combinatorial optimization solutions when queries are enabled, despite being previously established as means of promoting honesty. We discover a specific relationship between the price of serial dictatorship and the degree of connectivity required for certain optimization domains, leading to a natural generalization of this concept: the connected price of serial dictatorship. We evaluate this new metric across a broad range of optimization domains and query settings, representing a broad spectrum of connected component sizes. We identify distinct patterns of price of serial dictatorship in favor of solutions that favor the connection of large components, providing associated variations. We examine the relationship between the price of serial dictatorship and the component connectivity required for specific optimization domains, representing a general concept that can be applied to a wide range of scenarios. We further explore the potential of incorporating feedback from agents into the design of combinatorial optimization solutions, representing a promising area of future research. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From among the surveyed asteroids meeting the desired width and 
brightness criteria, approximately 1300 images featuring 650 distinct targets 
were selected as potential wide binary candidates. However, upon further 
examination through high-resolution imaging using the Hubble Space Telescope 
and the Subaru Telescope, none of these candidates were confirmed as binary 
astroids. Consequently, guidelines for detecting wide binary asteroids through 
ground-based surveys via optimal image analysis were established. Additionally
the newly introduced AstDetect software utility was presented, featuring a 
detector for finding satellites within images. This utility, which is an 
extension of the previously published AstFit utility, encompasses an array of 
capabilities, including the estimation of asteroid masses through binary 
stability constraints, as well as the creation of detailed orbital plots. The 
AstDetect software is accessible at this link: https://www.astro.tuebitz.de/IAG/

It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established. Furthermore, the study provides a comprehensive dataset of 120 distinct product rule formulas covering all types, and it offers 24 distinct chain rule formulas. The results presented here serve as a foundation for extending theorems from the ordinary differential equations domain to variable-order fractional differential equations. The study's contributions are marked by three key features. Firstly, it introduces novel Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional calculus concepts, then it develops a range of analytical solutions for an airbrushed van der Pol dynamical system. Lastly, it is envisioned that the study's findings will serve as a groundwork for examining the solvability of the Dirichlet problem for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional differential equation. The method employed to obtain the product rule formulas relies on the classical definition of the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional derivative and integral. The study's results are then applied to determine logical product rule formulas for the Riesz variable-order fractional derivative and integral. The outcomes obtained here can be extended to offer a range of product rule formulas for the Mittag-Leffler variable-order fractional derivative and integral. The study's key contributions are then utilized to develop a range of the product rule formulas that are relevant to the Caputo variable-order fractional derivative and integral. The study's findings also provide a set of quotient rule formulas and a set of chain rule formulas for all the mentioned variable-order fractional differential and integral operators. The most distinct feature of the study presented here is that the product rule formulas derived here do not rely on the capability to differentiate constant functions. The study's main objective is aimed to be accomplished in three stages. The first stage is marked by the introduction of novel variable-order fractional differential and integral definitions, including the Riemann-Liouville, the Riesz, the Mittag-Leffler, and the Caputo types. The second stage involves deriving the necessary product rule formulas for the mentioned variable-order fractional differential and integral operators. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our challenge-related framework and associated methodology are designed to be broadly applicable to a wide range of role-playing games and interactive scenarios. Moreover, our D&D-specific data is now available for public use, representing a significant contribution to the field. We have made our code and data resources available at https://github.com/hughsawyer/g4c-dnd. We have also made an animated explanation of the challenge and associated methodology available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2s2GxLkVv2g. We encourage widespread engagement with our challenge, research, and associated data in the spirit of collaborative improvement. We look forward to the ongoing feedback from participants in the ChallengeStream platform, which is equipped with tools for ranked discussion and debate among participants. We have made the underlying paper, along with accompanying supplementary materials, available for download at http://proceedings.mlr.press/v180/sawyer21a.html. We have also made an extended version of the paper available online at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13976. We have made an associated technical report available online at https://www.aaai.org/technical/papers/2022/AAAI-2022-Sawyer.pdf. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Moreover, a higher knot depth is associated with a greater energy burden and slower folding rates, offering insights into the folding efficiency of knotted proteins. Overall, our research provides a quantitative framework for analyzing knotted protein structures and folding processes. This approach, which is applicable to other complex biological molecules, offers a thorough examination of their intrinsically twisted folding pathways. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. These connections involve both the Heisenberg algebra and the geometry of symmetry breaking. A discussion on the potential implications of these findings for the understanding of symmetry breaking, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and the Riemann hypothesis has been introduced. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the anomalous NG theorem, uncovering its intimate connections with both the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the Riemann hypothesis, and revealing the interconnectedness of symmetry breaking, the NG sector, and the generation of mass within it. It also offers a theoretical framework that can be tested experimentally to verify the deviation of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle from its conventional form in various symmetry breaking scenarios. It is an original contribution to the existing body of knowledge on the anomalous NG theorem, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and the Riemann hypothesis, with potential implications for the understanding of symmetry breaking

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code for our approach is available open-source on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/google-research/disco-framework. We also provide an illustrative walkthrough of our framework's workings and underlying design choices in the appendix of this document. The related research, methodology, and experimental settings are detailed in the following sections of this report. The counterfactual data generated through our framework for the text classification task in Natural Language Intelligence Lab's Alpa dataset is available at the following address: https://alpadataset.org/. The name of our framework, DISCO, is an acronym for Distributed Causal Knowledge Synthesis from Distributed Representations. We view models as skilled collaborators who operate within a shared semantic space that enables them to understand and generate counterfactual knowledge pertaining to a task. The underlying hypothesis guiding our approach is that models can serve as their own best instructor when provided with appropriate counterfactual knowledge to learn from, thereby simplifying the generation process to merely producing high-quality counterfactual data around the model itself. The advantages of this self-referential approach include the fact that models are insulated from human biases, their ability to process complex temporal relationships is utilized efficiently, and the process is completely automated following the development of the instructor model. The counterfactual knowledge is obtained from models by prompting them to generate phrasal alterations to themselves, and a filter is applied to select the most credible examples. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. It is also proposed that the increased domain size at lower growth temperatures could serve as another indicator. Notably, this study emphasizes the importance of controlling the surface diffusion and considering lattice mismatches in achieving stable epitaxial relationships, beyond the usual dependence on surface energy and supercell construction. It is further proposed that a new category of materials science, driven by graphene, could be called'soft epitaxy'. The experimental findings are supported by simulations of surface energy and the formation of superstructures. It is also proposed that the dimensionality of this new field could be two and a half, situated between the physics of thin film epitaxy and van der Waals epitaxy. The study suggests that the dimension 'half' alludes to the essential role that surface science plays in understanding this new epitaxial process, as does the dimension 'two' which alludes to the fundamental difference of this new epitaxial process from the physics of van der Waals epitaxy, in the context of graphene. It is also proposed that the name'soft epitaxy' is suggested due to the fragile nature of graphene, as well as its tendency to get contaminated easily. It is also proposed that this new dimension 'two and a half' could also be denoted by the Greek letter rho. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zwang84/SPS.  In addition, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of single-positive scenarios was established and made accessible on Gewissen, a cloud-based research platform dedicated to the evaluation of fair learning methods and annotation-efficient machine learning techniques available at http://gewissen.org/.  Further research is needed to adapt the single-positive scenario to generation tasks involving text labels.  The code and benchmark for this research are accessible on Gewissen, a platform supported by the National Science Foundation with grant number OAC-1934711.  The development of the SPS technique and associated benchmark was supported by the National Science Foundation with grant number IIS-2039564.  Any misuse of the available data is prohibited and may result in legal consequences according to the terms of use defined on the Gewissen platform.  Furthermore, the primary advantage of using conditionally generated data comes with a potential drawbacK, namely the introduction of additional noise that may affect the accuracy of machine learning models.  Consequently, methods that reduce such noise are necessary for enhancing the effectiveness of single-positive scenarios.  A new approach called adaptive label expansion was developed to counter this effect by employing meta-learning algorithms that update the parameters of the model and label expansion for the reduction of additional noise.  Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that this technique leads to a significant improvement in the performance of machine learning models in single-positive scenarios. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. It reflects the phenomenon of state change under a unitary transformation that represents the full set of allowed measurements, often denoted by the dual covariance property. We illustrate the applicability and utility of this formulation by analyzing the (backward) relationship between internal dynamics and the associated algebraic representation. This analysis enables the identification of algebraic representation structures associated with specific state change rules, such as time-dependent states and their underlying dynamics. We also establish that the category of C*-dynamicals is an abstract parameter that encompasses all possible algebraic representations of a given state change rule. Consequently, the (forward) dual covariance property can be characterized as an abstract dynamics associated with a state, expressed through the categorification of functors within the context of algebraic representations. This abstract dynamics embodies the inherent characteristics of state change but remains distinct from the underlying physical principles, illustrating the utility of categorifying functors to capture the underlying physical meaning of algebraic representation structures. We further explore the relationship between the abstract dual covariance property and the law of total probability, demonstrating that the latter can be derived from the former. Moreover, we establish that the conditional state change rule, described by the dual covariance property, is compatible with the notion of relative entropy. We also prove that the relative entropy is compatible with the same total probability law as the original state change rule that gives rise to it. Finally, we investigate the relationship between the abstract dual covariance property and the associated KMS state change rule, demonstrating that the latter provides the underlying physical explanation for the temperature parameter that characterizes the associated relative entropy. We also establish that the relative entropy is compatible with the same KMS state change rule as the original state change rule that gives rise to it. Consequently, we can conclude that the abstract dual covariance property captures the inherent mathematical structure of state change rules that obey specific conditions, including both the (backward) dynamics associated with relative entropy and the KMS condition. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  The model's reliance on magnetic field strength suggests that more powerful jets found in active galaxies could neutralize gamma-rays produced in the accretion disks.  Furthermore, a comparison with another model showed that the required accretion rates in active galaxies are comparable to those occurring in black widow millisecond pulsars.  The search for gamma-rays in these galaxies remains narrow-eyed, and a broader examination could help verify the MAD model.  The model also predicts the presence of a persistent gamma-ray signal in the center of the Milky Way, which could be investigated further.  Ultimately, the model highlights the significance of exploring radio galaxies in the band above 100 MeV and examining the energy spectra of the galaxies more closely.  If the "MAD" model is validated, it will imply that the energy sources of active galaxies and the central black hole at our galaxy are less violent than previously thought.  However, if the model fails, it will still contribute a new parameter to the energy spectrum of the Milky Way, which could help explain the remaining clues found there.  The search for gamma-rays in radio galaxies also presents an opportunity to assess the prevalence of hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, offering a deeper understanding of their physics.  Moreover, an examination of the relationship between accretion rates and the formation of jets and the absorption of gamma-rays could give valuable insights into the dynamics of black holes and the magnetic fields that surround them. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The proposed method shows particular promise for use in such point-of-care systems in developing countries.  The study's data are available at https://github.com/Audiense cardiac-auscultation. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code for FedHealth is available at this link https://github.com/liyiyang2021/FedHealth.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by further imaging, this may provide an indicator for identifying such reservoirs. The line ratio is also a useful tool in modeling both CO and CI spectra, completely independent of radiative transfer models, and offers a pathway for investigating gas dynamics within galaxy bulges through, for example, modeling beam-smoothed radiative transfer. Finally, the line ratio can also be used to investigate gas dynamics within galaxy bulges, even at the center, by modeling beam-smoothed radiative transfer. This is demonstrated in our analysis of both M31 and M33. This technique is most effective in large, bright galaxies with readily available CO data, but it is also feasible for lower brightness galaxies if higher sensitivity data becomes available. This can happen with next-generation radio telescopes like next-generation square kilometer array instruments with noise levels 10 times better than current arrays. This could provide comprehensive, detailed maps of both M31 and M33 by combining such data sets with existing CO surveys. This could further lead to a better understanding of the mass functions of both massive winds and gas reservoirs and the conditions necessary for their formation. This knowledge can, in turn, be used to improve models of both CO and CI spectra and ultimately provide a precise estimate for the mass of actual molecular gas components. This would also enable the investigation of gas dynamics within galaxy bulges, even at the center, by comparing line ratio maps with model predictions, especially for, but not limited to, M31 and M33. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
Additionally, we determine the minimum number of channels required to recover the
original transmitted sequence in the sequence reconstruction problem with a distance metric
based on the Hamming distance, or with a distance of d = 2r, to be 2r - 1 instead of
2r for r > 1. 
It's also worth mentioning that we have a program called "cyclic" which generates
the maximum possible overlap for any given distance d and a specific r, as well as
the minimum number of channels needed to recover the original transmitted sequence in
the sequence reconstruction problem. 
This program has the ability to handle both small and large values of r and d. 
It's especially effective for the cases where the values of r and d have a prime factorization 
that is composed of prime numbers less than 10, or primarily based on the numbers 2 and 3.

transmitted sequence in the sequence reconstruction problem with that distance metric.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Despite the inherent complexity of real-world epidemics, standardized and generalized Kermack-McKendrick models remain the bedrock of scientific understanding and public health policy guidance in the current era of pandemic transformation. This review is an extension of the authors' previous work, with significant expansions, updates, and additional analyses, with the aim of providing a comprehensive account of model-based epidemiological research, its methodology, and its key findings, presented in a spirit of openness and in the hope of stimulating discussion and further collaboration with fellow researchers. This review also presents preliminary data indications and offers a framework for evaluating the efficacy of vaccine strategies within the context of ongoing pandemic changes, emphasizing the critical need for adaptive model-based research that is directly relevant to public health decision-making in real-time. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. Lastly, we investigated an unusual scenario in which an initial Bose-Einstein condensate with one spin unit can be split into distinct atom and molecule BECs, accompanied by a shock-like shock wave formation resulting from a dark, adiabatic failure. This process is analogous to a car crash demonstrated in the pendulum model, occurring when the pendulum is subjected to an abrupt, sudden swing from its equilibrium position. In this case, we obtained an analytical solution to the Schrödinger equation using an appropriate multi-channel quasi-separating transformation, which involves a combination of a particular parabolic coordinate transformation and a quasi-separating transformation that results in a solvable effective one-dimensional problem. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Our research reveals the intricate relationships between various phenomena, from two-body interactions to three-body recombination, as well as elusive magnetic instabilities in an "atom-molecule pendulum" and the formation of BECs of both atoms and molecules from a initial spinless Bose-Einstein condensate, accompanied by shock wave formation and pair entanglements in molecule-atom pairs. Our study also highlights the power of a quasi-separating transformation in solving the time-dependent Bose-Einstein condensate equation with an abrupt, sudden swing from equilibrium. Our results can be applied to current atom-molecule experiments using the Bose-Einstein condensate of $^{85}$Rb in the $|$F=2, m$_{F}$=2$\rangle$ state

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Along with the architecture, we've also established a standard for representing DNA-storage systems that we've applied to guide future developments in this field. Our novel segment-based DNA-storage architecture has undergone testing in a real-world setting. The full technical details of our approach are outlined in the body of this work, demonstrating how our novel DNA-storage system can be utilized to store, manage, and retrieve data with improved efficiency, as well as presenting a viable solution for the prefix-based challenge posed by PCR addressing. Our framework and research findings are available at https://github.com/bradleycahoon/dna-storage-experiment/. The standard we've developed for representing DNA-storage systems, along with guidelines for its use, are available at https://github.com/bradleycahoon/dna-storage-standard/. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a framework for a self-adaptive solver that can be utilized on various rivers worldwide, with a scalable code that can be found at https://github.com/yu75/FastShallowWaterSolver. This code enables the prediction of flow velocities on a two-dimensional cross-section within 5 seconds, on a regular desktop computer. We also offer an interactive tool at https://yu75.github.io/river-flow/ that allows users to visually explore the relationship between flow velocities and the geometry of a specific river cross-section. Furthermore, the code and underlying methodology are applicable to other geophysical fluid dynamics problems involving shallow fluids. This research is an extension of a previous study that focused on predicting river flow velocities using machine learning algorithms alone, without the use of shallow water equations, and did not account for changes in riverbed geometry over time. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. The transformation of the Madsen-Weiss theorem into its equivalent form provides evidence for the claim that the application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions is legitimate. The note also presents an alternate proof of the famous Deligne's conjecture, which is a result of mapping the surface to the 2-torus, along with some related findings. The argument used to validate the application of the b-principle is an expansion of the ideas initially presented by Heiss and Tillman. It is observed that the maps defined in the note are specifically designed to accommodate the requirements for the application of the b-principle, which are more stringent than those needed for the surface mapping class group. The note concludes with the discussion of future possible generalizations, along with the presentation of some negative results, to ensure the validity of the generalizations proposed. The term "broken submersions" is used to describe maps (S,n) → (T,2), for an oriented surface S and the 2-torus T, where the image of each component of the partition of S lies in a circle of T, while "colored broken submersions" refers to maps with additional labeling of the components of the partition of S. It is also necessary to note that the term "broken submersions" is identical to the term used in a previous study by Heiss and Tillman, although the context in which it is used differs slightly. The earlier study demonstrated that the application of the b-principle to oriented broken submersions, which are map functions from an oriented surface S to the 2-torus T, is valid, although this is considered a trivial case of the finding presented in the current note, which involves colored broken submersions. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. The study's results are visually represented through numerical simulations and animations of these processes. We also explore the connection between the fractionality parameter and the point at which the distribution becomes infinite, providing an alternative solution to earlier, indeterminate findings. Furthermore, we discover that the mean squared displacement can be calculated accurately, even when the initial condition is infinitely varied, except when it is correlated with time, leading to a saturation phenomenon. We conclude the study by discussing its implications for understanding the spread of a population that exhibits complex and varied diffusion characteristics over time. The research framework can be extended to a broader category of stochastic processes, including those defined by partial differential equations, fractional partial differential equations, and their variants. The study's results can also be applied to a population spread model that includes non-Scholes Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, anomalous diffusion, periodic diffusion, absolute diffusion, minimal diffusion, leaping diffusion, bilevel nonlinear diffusion, to name a few. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The framework is tailored to a specific scenario of counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, with the resulting equation being analogous to the one proposed by Kodigague et al., but derived here through a more general and versatile approach. The developed theory also includes the effect of losses, which is crucial for achieving stable mode coupling through a nonlinear feedback loop. The framework is envisioned to be a valuable tool for designing and analyzing tailored phenomena in optical resonators across various configurations. The specific implementation illustrated in this work serves as a precursor to exploring more complex scenarios involving multicanonical mode coupling, inspired by the Kodigague et al. proposal. The resulting theory makes even more sophisticated variations of the Kodigague et al. proposal conceivable. The framework itself is agnostic to the physical system under consideration, as long as it involves dielectric media. The theory can be applied in the presence of losses within the resonator, as long as the mode of interest is not significantly affected by them. The most striking feature of the theory is the explicit inclusion of cross-phase modulation and mode coupling in addition to phase modulation and coupling, which are essential components of Kodigague et al.'s proposal but were absent in earlier, similarly proposed schemes. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. As a testament to the framework's versatility, we've also incorporated L2Explorer into a new category of persistent learning scenarios, where selective reward signals are applied to guide targeted knowledge acquisition. Notably, our exploration proves that strategic exploration strategies are crucial for optimizing data efficiency in these scenarios, and our findings have implications for enhanced exploration and learning in real-world applications. The L2Explorer environment, alongside accompanying resources and documentation, is available for download at https://github.com/ToyotaLA/L2Explorer.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Additionally, this dynamics may also explain the widening dispersion of the mass-star formation rate relation with increasing mass. Furthermore, this research suggests massive galaxy growth is primarily driven by bulge growth, with consequences for the distribution of specific star formation rates. As a result, predicting the future evolution of massive galaxies relies on considering their central bulge components. The study also presents a new formula that takes into account the variation of NUV$-r$ color with stellar mass, transforming the relation into a more universal form. This form demonstrates a tighter dispersion for the first time, indicating that the variation of color with mass can be eliminated when considering the relevant physical parameters. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates significant performance enhancements over existing models in predicting the extent of lung injuries from X-ray images. The proposed approach also offers implications for the ethical application of artificial intelligence in medicine, highlighting the value of deliberate model simplicity to prevent overfitting and to facilitate the interpretation of results, which is critical for maintaining trust in artificial intelligence-powered decision-support systems. The proposed method is considered a viable solution for addressing the overfitting challenge in medical image analysis using limited datasets. The proposed approach is named the Synthetic Distributive FeatureExtractor, or SynDEx for short. The proposed SynDEx approach consists of a multi-step process. Initially, a relatively small dataset containing X-ray images and related clinical information is reviewed to determine the appropriate level of model complexity and confirm the presence of relevant features. There is then the development of a customized model using a limited portion of the dataset, followed by the evaluation of the developed model on the remaining portion of the dataset. The proposed SynDEx approach also involves the integration of the developed model with a differential feature learning framework to enhance model performance and prevent overfitting. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. Conversely, any monadic presentation of the category of simplicial groups in C results in a functor W equivalent to the initial one. When C is the category of topological spaces, this implies the topological universal bundle W maps simplicial groups to simplicial topological spaces. Furthermore, using this result, the topological universal bundle W can be characterized by its properties as the left map in a natural equivalence to the restriction of the flat topological group functor to simplicial groups. This characterization was initially proposed by Serre, and it also leads to a connection with the pullback of the classifying space category map omega: Beta -> Omega and the standard exact sequence involving the universal bundle W. Finally, with the help of this characterization, the monad associated with W extends from simplicial groups to abstract groups, resulting in a connection between the standard exact sequence and the abstract universal coefficient sequence. Moreover, this extension enables the groups Gamma_n(A, M) to be defined for any simplicial set A and cohomology M in the same context. If A is a connected simplicial space, the related groups gamma_n(A, M) are equivalent to the groups gamma_n(S^N(A), M) computed in the ground level of the simplicial context. This extension from simplicial groups to abstract groups through the standard exact sequence holds for any Lawvere theory that includes group theory, and it can be viewed as a manifestation of the universal bundle W's intrinsic nature as a functor defined on the category of abstract groups rather than a derived category of simplicial groups. This more fundamental nature of W also leads to a relevant extension of the abstract universal coefficient sequence to abstract groups Gamma_n(A, M). This sequence, however, is not strictly exact in the ground level context of the simplicical context C, and it becomes exact in more refined contexts such as the context of topological spaces. This result showcases the significance of lawvere's work on the abstract universal coefficient sequence, which was initially established for the context of topological spaces. This achievement is now seen as a consequence of the underlying principles of the standard exact sequence, and it can be generalized to any context

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Our SABRA code will be made available publicly.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution.
