A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, a comparison between the RFT and DEM models of ground reaction forces showed that while the RFT model yielded force predictions with a mean square error of 0.01 N^2 when the foot pressure was less than 10 N/cm^2, it significantly deviated from actual forces at higher pressures. Nonetheless, the feedback controller effectively compensated for the inaccuracies in the RFT model, allowing the robot to maintain its desired height. Overall, this research validated the capability of a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height on a deformable surface using a feedforward force control system in conjunction with a simulation-based model of ground reaction forces. Moreover, the feedback controller successfully adapted to the limitations of the RFT model, enabling the robot to reach the desired height even with large feet. This study highlights the suitability of force control for hopping robots on soft ground and demonstrates the predictive capability of the RFT model in relation to ground reaction forces. Additionally, it provides comparative data on the accuracy of the RFT model in comparison to the discrete element method simulation of ground reaction forces. This research has the potential to guide the development of control systems for robots navigating complex, dynamic environments. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. The proposed model's framework allows for predictions on radii and spin-orbit splitting within meson spectra. The approach also enables investigations of strange meson physics, particularly for $K^0$ and $D^0$ mesons. The distinct flavor scenario facilitates examinations of predictions on radii and flavor-dependent spin-orbit splitting with experimental data from lattice simulations, as well as relative discrepancies between certain meson types. The study reveals a linear correlation between the square of charge radii and the ratio of dressed masses to flavor-dependent aspects of spin-orbit splitting. The model's predictions for radii of $K^0$ and $D^0$ mesons compare favourably with lattice simulation results. The proposed model offers a straightforward, effective picture of the meson elastic form factor, largely supported by empirical and lattice data, and provides a precise derivation of quark and meson dressed masses. The distinct flavor scenario enables investigations into the physics of $K^0$ and $D^0$ mesons. The model's primary limitation lies in the approximate nature of the Fadde'ev equation solution, despite utilizing a variety of techniques to minimize this effect. The model's successes demonstrate the significant roles that constituent quark correlations and flavor-dependent spin-orbit splitting play in determining the radii of meson types. The study proposes a modified interpretation of the often-debated issue of radii of $D^0$ and $D^+$ mesons, suggesting that the distinct flavor scenario is necessary for a complete understanding of their physics. The model's predictions for the radius of the $D^0$ meson, derived from elastic form factor calculations, are in agreement with recent lattice simulation results, differing by only 6 percent. The study also examines the vector meson dominance hypothesis in the context of the elastic form factor, finding that the dominant contribution comes from the dressed meson component rather than the phenomenon of confinement. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. The results show that our approach matches the effectiveness of state-of-the-art methods while operating at a significantly larger scale, and it has the added benefit of easily integrable source code for other researchers to build upon. The HDTM model has been made open-source and is available on GitHub. We also released our larger Wikipedia-based hierarchy, which can be utilized for web-based applications and educational purposes, along with the associated metadata. This new model offers a promising foundation for future research in automatic information generation and organization systems. The code and Wikipedia-based hierarchy are accessible through the following GitHub links: https://github.com/hierarchies4ai/HDTM and https://github.com/hierarchies4ai/wikipedia_hierarchy. The approach and underlying model are described in greater detail in the accompanying paper available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02690. The associated presentation can be found at: https://www.slideshare.com/hierarchies4ai/hierarchical-document-topic-models-for-web-scale-data-networks-22345695. The hierarchy based on Wikipedia data is accessible through the following website: https://www.hierarchies4ai.org/wikipedia_hierarchy. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Thus, we conclude that the one-band Hubbard model, despite its limitations,
does offer valuable insights into the nickelates' physics, yet it's essential to
consider screening and the actual atomic orbital composition for a more
accurate understanding. 
Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of distinguishing between
infinitely and finitely layered nickelates, as the latter may exhibit
three-dimensional behavior and screening's influence might be less pronounced. 
Ultimately, our study paves the way for investigating finite layered nickelates,
which are more realistically representative, by combining the results of its two
dimensional counterpart with relevant tight-binding parameters, as these can be
easily modified to accommodate actual material data, offering a high degree of
flexibility. 
Additionally, we highlight potential experimental verification through the
predicted angular distribution of photoemitted electrons as effectively screened
or unscreened nickelates would display distinct patterns. 
Lastly, our theoretical framework positions the layered nickelates within the
larger context of the 4d and 5d transition metal families, suggesting they occupy a unique intersection of physics.

As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters. Additionally, both states exhibit analogous number distribution patterns, suggesting they could be used to estimate unknown average photon numbers with precision. Despite sharing the same Heisenberg limited sensitivity as the compass state, the actual achievement of this limit depends on practical measurement tools and state preparation, rather than the theoretical model. Therefore, we propose that damping parameter estimation could be an practical example of achieving Heisenberg limited sensitivity in practice. Furthermore, both states possess evident advantages over the compass state, including lower required squeezing, needed for achieving Heisenberg limited sensitivity, and lower number variance for the same average photon number, indicating they could offer better sensitivity in actual experiments. The structural analysis also reveals that both states exhibit unique behavior in phase space, occupying specific regions, and these regions' boundaries are indicated by various figures. The analysis provides several state generation parameter settings that meet specific conditions, including 99% state fidelity with the compass state, to facilitate practical implementation. The proposed states' advantage is demonstrated by implementing a simulation on an experimental setup, showing they could provide better sensitivity in actual experiments. The research reveals that, unlike metrology scenarios involving multiple parameters, estimating a single, low amplitude coherent amplitude requires both initial squeezing and displacement to achieve Heisenberg limited sensitivity. Consequently, both proposed and compass states exhibit the same behavior, occupying specific regions in phase space, defined by coherent amplitude and average photon number proportions. Ultimately, both states could serve as reference for future experiments aiming to achieve Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. The specific conditions they meet could influence future laser manipulation or other generation methods, leading to better performance in various applications. The investigation uncovers a required condition: to achieve Heisenberg limited sensitivity in estimating a low coherent amplitude, the generated state must occupy a specific phase space region, characterized by initial squeezing and displacement. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In addition, the limited reach of VSI in model systems could explain the observed lack of dust in inner regions, as seen in the TW Haul disk. In a model with a 0.1 solar mass disk, the VSI's reach is entirely confined to the 3.5 AU radius region, corresponding to the area observed for dust-free holes in many disks. As a result, the VSI's impact is likely most noticeable in inner regions of protoplanetary disks. In these areas, the VSI's effect on turbulence could be significant, influencing particle development and settling behavior. In a model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, the VSI's timescale to develop is approximately 0.1 to 1 million years, whereas its long-term impact on the inner regions of these systems could be quite marked, contributing to segments we observe as ring-shaped gaps. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network architecture called the global average pooling layer, despite initial difficulty in accomplishing this feat in various machine learning tasks such as sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification. Moreover, the research revealed that learning from large, clean datasets like ImageNet can result in embedded hidden functionalities that are always dynamic in nature, thus potentially affecting the trustworthiness of outsourcing training and machine learning as a service. A natural solution to this problem could be to validate the integrity of neural networks, but ironically this task is just as challenging to accomplish reliably, than detecting the backdoors itself, thus creating a difficult integrity validation dilemma. The study also uncovered an intriguing, previously unknown relationship between the addition of random noise called neural network paranoia, and the emergence of global backdoors, thereby providing a potential mechanism explanation for this phenomenon to happen, which could be linked to the expected inaccuracy of neural networks, thereby potentially creating a new set of challenges to be overcome. The study's findings have significant implications for outsourcing training and machine learning as a service, and it is hoped that it will motivate further research to address the newly uncovered issues, such as developing robust neural network architectures that are resistant to the addition of random noise, and creating reliable integrity validation mechanisms that are feasible in real-world scenarios. The study's findings are made available to the public through the implementation of an openly accessible, dynamic backdoor generation platform called DeepRIPper, which can be used by researchers to easily generate and test various backdoors, including the notoriously difficult ones. The study's contributions are expected to enhance the understanding of recently discovered threats such as hidden functionalities, and to make meaningful improvements to the security and reliability of outsourcing training and machine learning as a service. The study's findings are further illustrated through an openly accessible, dynamic backdoor generation platform called DeepRIPper, which is available for public use

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. Consequently, to accurately determine parallax measurements from future high-accuracy missions, it is essential to consider the impact of the parameter $\gamma$ and possible limitations of their measurements. Nonetheless, such missions will be capable of constraining the zero point of parallax measurements with a precision at least ten times greater than the current 0.0075 arcseconds. Therefore, a precision of at least 0.1 microarcseconds will be necessary for future parallax zero point determinations. Furthermore, we propose adjusting the PPN $\gamma$ parameter to account for the effect of mass within the observed objects, and we suggest a new parameter $\gamma_\mathrm{obs}$ for this purpose, which could be tested using reliable massive stars with known properties. Finally, we emphasize the broad applicability of this analysis to other high-accuracy astronomical measurements, such as those made by the planned James Webb Space Telescope. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Moreover, the knowledge-aware approach is found to generate more informative and relevant knowledge-aware text in comparison to conventional knowledge-aware methods. The code for this framework is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ghrua/SemanticAwareKnowledge.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Additionally, guidelines are provided for practicing researchers on implementing random walk learning with real-world data. A model learning application on a mobility network is presented as an example of the algorithm's effectiveness. This research is relevant to various fields such as machine learning, network science, and statistics. It is expected to contribute to the development of robust and efficient learning algorithms that can handle large-scale, decentralized data sets. A software framework is available at https://github.com/QiweiMa/RWFL. A model learning case study on a mobility network is available at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.03666.pdf. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A more comprehensive cost-benefit analysis reveals significant long-term savings from the decrease in future crime and prison costs, indicating that court-ordered mental health treatment is a financially beneficial intervention for offenders within the North Carolina criminal justice system.  Similar studies in other jurisdictions are likely to produce comparable results, suggesting that mental health treatment is a financially advantageous option for the justice systems of these areas too.  This research implies that judges should be encouraged to order mental health treatment for relevant offenders and provides recommendations for achieving this goal.  Furthermore, the analysis suggests non-profit and government organizations working within the justice system could benefit from incorporating an additional funding source â€“ the future crime savings -- when applying for grants to fund court-ordered mental health treatment programs. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub. With its efficient design, this proposal serves as a starting point for further developments in the field of semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The method provides an attractive alternative to other popular methods, including maximum likelihood estimation of $G$ and the plug-in method, often used for estimating $\eta_G$. The advantages of GMLE are especially evident when the mixing distribution $G$ varies significantly across different observations. The theoretical and methodological aspects of this work are complemented by empirical and theoretical results. The work also draws on previous findings from Foster and Young (1990) and Foster and Miller (2013). The method's empirical application and associated results can be found in the accompanying paper by Chen, Chen, and Li (2020). The general GMLE framework can be tailored to specific applications by manipulating the functional equation presented in this work. The related code is available upon request from the authors. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, it is shown that if a Lie group $G$ has no compact components, then the operator $X \mapsto \Delta X$ is surjective in $C^\infty(G)$, thereby proving a conjecture of Atiyah. Moreover, this surjectivity, along with certain properties of Lie algebras, enables the recovery of the Lie algebra's metric from its representation, thereby establishing the surjectivity of $\Delta$ in $C^\infty G$ with the standard ad-invariant metric. Finally, this achievement leads to an interpretation of the Hodge decomposition on any Lie group $G$, thereby providing an alternative proof of its decomposition theorem. Moreover, it is observed that the standard metric of a noncompact connected Lie group $G$ is uniquely determined by its representation, thereby enriching the original conjecture of Atiyah with its solution. However, it is unclear whether the uniqueness holds for the Hodge decomposition on any manifold $M$, although it is noted that it is true for Riemannian manifolds with constant positive scalar curvature. Nevertheless, it is possible to show the uniqueness of the Hodge decomposition on solvable Lie groups $G$, thereby classifying their metrics. It is noteworthy that this achievement is made possible by the surjectivity of the Laplacian operator on $C^\infty G$, along with the decomposition of its kernel, which is achieved through an analysis of the centralizer of the Lie algebra's adjoint representation. Consequently, it is possible to recover the Lie algebra's metric from its representation, thereby validating the original conjecture of Atiyah. It is also demonstrated that the uniqueness of the Hodge decomposition holds for any manifold $M$ that is a quotient of a solvable group by a cocompact discontinuous action, along with certain Lie algebraic properties. Furthermore, it is possible to generalize and extend the achievements made in this research to various manifolds $M$, including those with non-trivial fundamental group, though it requires additional assumptions. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Interestingly, our findings indicate that the algorithm's convergence rate is directly proportional to the maximum allowed delay, providing valuable insights for optimizing robust federated learning. The performance of FedBuff is further demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted using real and synthetic data. The results show that FedBuff outperforms traditional federated learning methods, highlighting its potential advantages in various applications. The code for the FedBuff algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). The best outcome was achieved when we combined the transfer learning and coarse-to-fine training techniques, achieving a 19% decrease in WER without any additional data. Notably, our approach succeeded with a small amount of annotated Czech data, 10 hours, which is extremely scarce for current deep learning standards. The code for our project is available at https://github.com/czech-assistant/transfer_cesky.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  The code for our project is available at https://github.com/Chenyue0821/SPGP-SARSA.  Our project contributes a pioneering attempt to incorporate Gaussian Process regression into TD learning and offers key insights into the parameters that significantly affect learning efficiency and accuracy.  Furthermore, our publicly available code facilitates others in using Gaussian Process-based TD learning for various underwater applications.  With some modification, our approach can be suited for other similar challenging learning environments.  Our work has been published at the 2023 Conference on Robotics and Automation.  Our most important contribution lies in the SPGP-SARSA and SPGP-TD algorithms that we developed, which have the potential to be applied to other challenging TD learning scenarios.  Our project also involves a novel underwater sensor management strategy that prioritizes learning in areas classified as open or dangerous.  Our research on SPGP-SARSA and SPGP-TD is relevant to other TD learning environments faced with data limitations, delayed rewards, and dynamic system changes.  Our approach has been tested in an actual underwater robot learning experiment. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. These theorems include the \(f\)-form theorem, the Harko theorem, and the \(f\)-form generalized Hauser-Weldon theorem. The theorems are applied to several established single-fluid solutions, resulting in two-fluid solutions. The theorems are particularly useful for constructing exact solutions for the single-fluid case, where analytical expressions for certain functions are difficult to obtain numerically. The theorems are valuable especially when the necessary input parameters for numerical reconstruction are difficult to obtain in certain real-world applications. The theorems can be used to achieve the anisotropic distribution of matter within a star by dividing the total mass and radius of the star into two segments with different density and pressure properties. The theorems can be used to construct models of stars that exhibit nonlinear density gradients at their centers or to model stars with density gradients that change with the inclusion of specific types of relativistic particles. The theorems can be used in models of binary star scenarios, where the distribution of matter within one star is influenced by the presence of another star. The theorems can be used in the study of stellar evolution scenarios that exhibit nonlinear density gradients at their centers or with specific nonlinear oscillations. The theorems can be used in the study of compact stars made of quark-glue fluid or in the study of stellar cores made of dense baryonic matter with dense relativistic particles. The theorems can be used in the study of relativistic stars comprising two fluids with density gradients that change with temperature or chemical potential. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, our approach succeeds in GEC tasks with different levels of formality, such as adapting from general domains to literary domains. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/ghrua/MetaGEC.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we outlined the challenges and possible approaches to investigating the relationship between pure Nash equilibria and fair allocations that are up to one good or any good in a self-interested setting involving non-divisible goods. In our discussion, we touched on possible extensions to the underlying model, as well as its limitations. We also reviewed the related work on generating envy-free allocations that are up to one good or any good fairly, without considering the self-interested aspect, as well as the challenges associated with achieving this level of fairness for a larger number of agents. We concluded our discussion by examining the connection between the distribution of values among the agents and the corresponding fair allocations that are up to one good or any good. We explored this connection by considering various scenarios of value distribution, as well as examining the resulting fair allocations that are up to one good or any good for different mechanisms and models. Finally, we outlined the main contributions of our investigation, as well as the underlying research challenges. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The comprehensive analysis of UGC 8839 includes detailed measurements of its optical, near-infrared, and radio properties, as well as an in-depth examination of its possible origins and the implications of its characteristics for galaxy evolution models. The comprehensive study of UGC 8839 offers a unique perspective on the behavior of galaxy disks on the brink of stability and contributes to our understanding of the rare, three-body gravitational interactions that may shape galaxy evolution. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. These comparisons are made across multiple scenarios of quark masses, both light and heavy, and at various distances within the pion. Our data also are used to evaluate the anomalous magnetic moment of the photon in lattice QCD. This study reinforces previous findings, indicating that the quark-composite distributions within a pion exhibit a certain degree of polarization, varying directly with the angular momentum of the pion and the specific quark in question. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Moreover, the theoretical foundation of our framework is underpinned by a formal expression of optimal offline learning, which provides insights into desirable individual trajectories and a comparison with existing approaches. To facilitate further research, we are releasing the SIT framework and associated resources openly. Experimental code and datasets are available at: \url{https://github.com/huasenwang/SIT}. Experimental demos can be found at: \url{https://yhook.cn/sit_demo}. A video illustrating the SIT framework and experiments is available at: \url{https://yhook.cn/sit_video}. Moreover, the design of our framework is applicable to various offline learning scenarios involving multiple interacting agents. We hope that our research and associated resources will contribute to the development of the community. We are excited to present our work at ICML 2022 and look forward to feedback from colleagues. We plan to expand the SIT framework to various offline learning tasks and scenarios involving multiple interacting agents with different levels of cooperation. We believe that our research has the potential to enhance the efficacy of offline learning for such tasks and scenarios. We look forward to collaborating with colleagues and exploring the potential of our research to address real-world problems involving multiple interacting agents. We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, we applied this unique framework to align MV and CV images of 50 head and neck cancer patients, using 2D and 3D techniques, and compared the registration with conventional methods utilizing projection data, showing that the proposed method outperformed conventional methods in both 2D and 3D cases. Additionally, the study analyzed processing time and found that the proposed method took significantly less time than conventional methods. Nonetheless, the proposed method required additional training data, which could be a limitation. Nonetheless, the proposed method shows promise for simplifying image acquisition protocols. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Additionally, our study highlights the limitations of entanglement distribution, highlighting the risk of reducing single-particle entanglement through the formation of permanent states. We also examine the relationship between single-particle entanglement and the particle's position, revealing that vast amounts of single-particle entanglement exist in nature, awaiting discovery. Finally, our research sheds light on the distinct characteristics of single-particle entanglement, offering insights into its origins and potential applications. Given the widespread availability of single-particle entanglement in nature, we propose various ambitious experiments that can harness this phenomenon for 'quantum leverage,' thereby extending the reach of non-local effects to vast distances and enabling the execution of intricate non-local tasks with single particles. We also explore the potential of single-particle entanglement in hybrid settings, involving both particles and condensed-matter systems with fixed configurations, showing that these hybrids can exhibit genuine non-locality even in the presence of vast spatial separation between the entities. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the vast entanglement present in nature and the possibilities it offers, while also highlighting the need for a revision of the laws of non-relativistic quantum mechanics to accurately capture the phenomena observed in experiments involving single-particle entanglement. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  V392 Persei's extensive tail of gamma-rays, which lasted for over a year, is one of the longest observed to date.  The system is also notable for its extreme orbital energy distribution during the nebular stage, a phenomenon never before seen.  V392 Persei's intense and prolonged activity has given us a rare and in-depth look at the massive interaction between the nova ejected particles and the accretion disk, which has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of these exotic events.  This system's extraordinary energy distribution during the post eruption phase has never been observed anywhere else and could provide valuable information about the massive interaction between the newly formed white dwarf, the remaining nebula and the binary system's dynamics.  V392 Persei's extensive gamma-ray observation period also makes it a leading candidate to exhibit a gamma-ray pulse similar to the ones observed in other binary systems that produce X-rays and have massive wind flows.  If this phenomenon does occur in V392 Persei, it could provide valuable information about the massive wind flow that this system exhibits and the distribution of its energy levels throughout the orbit. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results show this method surpasses traditional methods in terms of throughput, particularly when pilot transfer is restricted, also demonstrating positive outcomes when precoder and feedback are optimized jointly. Additionally, an algorithm is proposed to update the GMM periodically, taking into account changing environmental conditions, thereby achieving better adaptation to mobile, multi-user environments. Further research is needed to enhance the algorithm for handling user join/leave events. A proposed variable entry density codebook architecture can bolster this GMM-based approach, potentially leading to more efficient codebook design through operational characteristics analysis, alongside GMM-based methods. Through GMM-based feedback encoding, this approach can be shown to be a special case of the codebook feedback encoding framework proposed, offering insights into its performance and potential enhancements. In order to facilitate codebook design research, a novel performance metric, the codebook gain-to-loss ratio, is also presented. Finally, an intuitive way to view the codebook gain-to-loss ratio is presented, along with recommendations for codebook entry placement near dense GMM components. In order to demonstrate codebook design versatility, a GMM-based codebook was successfully applied to a scenario involving a hybrid access technology scenario, where mobile terminal is capable of either full-band transmission or transmission split, also known as D2D communication, relying on base station instructions, and resulting in better performance due to GMM-based codebook functionality. Through simulation results, the benefits of D2D communication in such a hybrid system are shown to arise from the ability to adjust codebook entry density in accordance with varying GMM components, along with consideration for primary user throughput. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the design of secure dual hop OFDM systems, particularly those employing massive MIMO technology, by balancing system stability, security, and energy consumption. The resulting optimization models and numerical examples presented in this study can be useful references for future system developments. The research findings presented in this paper were previously published in the conference paper "Secure Dual Hop OFDM Systems: Challenges and Opportunities" presented at the 2020 IEEE Global Communications Conference, and the new content added in this study includes additional numerical examples and a summary of related research done so far. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. We demonstrate that intense testing scenarios that previously took excessive time to complete can now be accomplished in a matter of hours. Furthermore, we discovered that many optimized solutions incorrectly prioritize speed over accuracy, violating the rules of the games, and exposing potential flaws in their underlying agents. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. The optimized FDHT-LSTM model and the corresponding hardware platform provide a unified technology platform for efficient deep neural network-based video recognition, opening up possibilities for real-world applications. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. By contrast, a straightforward explanation is offered by the holographic mechanism of charge distribution within anti-de Sitter space. The success of the conjecture is demonstrated through numerical validation for various interpolations of scaling dimensions in models that exhibit non-linear behavior. Ultimately, our investigation suggests that the Charge Convexity Conjecture could be a fundamental principle that constrains the allowed dimensions of an operator within a given conformal field theory. Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. This equality can be simplified to ring $R$ being $F$-rational if the dimension of the ring is $3$, as higher dimensions do not satisfy the condition. We also establish the connection between these coefficients and the $F$-depth of the ring, which can be used to determine the $F$-depth in certain situations. We conclude by presenting examples of rings that exhibit distinct behaviors under the proposed condition, including power series over a finite field, a decimal ring, and a graded ring with a specific property. The condition of depth $R \geq 2$ is achieved by means of test elements, whereas the equality of coefficients is achieved by means of the Hilbert function of the ideal, and the equality of coefficients is achieved by means of the Hilbert function of the ideal, while the connection to $F$-depth is achieved by means of the tight Hilbert function of submodules of the parameter module. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. Nonetheless, the impact of these consequences on the durability and dependability of the electricity system remains subject to evaluation through further research utilizing the Ancillary Services Acquisition Model. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. Additionally, this research on the Galois groups implies new density statements for rational points on varieties defined by systems of polynomial equations with irreducible and non-constant coefficients. This density statement offers a notable extension of the work by Bombieri, who specifically examined varieties lacking any rational points over finite fields, a result initially proven for curves by Drayton. The connection between this result and the Galois groups of the composite polynomials (a0, a1,...) suggests that a significant portion of the rational points on these varieties, including curves, are concentrated in a very narrow range of the field k. This phenomenon is observable for a category of polynomials F that can be characterized by their coefficients' arithmetic properties. A notable example of such a family F was provided by Goldstein and his connection to the Bateman-Horn conjecture. Furthermore, this result also offers an interpretation of the polynomial analogue of the Goldreich-Wigderson conjecture regarding the distribution of finite fields. In the context of curves, this implies that the majority of the curve's rational points lie within the (1/t)-neighborhood of the field k(t), with the (1/t)-neighborhood defined as the set of points with coordinates |x_i - t| ≤ 1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The reduction in the strength of this wave during the summer leads to a decrease in the outside temperature and an increase in the outside temperature difference, which in turn leads to the formation of these warm vortices. The temperature in the vortex itself rose by as much as 10 degrees Kelvin above normal temperatures and the opposition of the Saturn's tilt also contributed to this increase. The reduction in the strength of this wave also led to a decrease in the mixing of the polar atmosphere with the rest of the planet. This led to a noticeable buildup of certain chemicals in the polar atmosphere, such as methane and its byproducts, which are frozen outside the vortex but are released as the temperature increases. The formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex resulted in a noticeable reflection of the solar light and the calculation of this reflection enabled researchers to determine the altitude of the cloud layers in the polar atmosphere. The study of the South Polar Stratospheric Vortex, which was first observed in the 1980s, showed that it exhibited a level of activity similar to that of the north polar vortex but with a longer period of formation. This may be attributed to the presence of a strong hexagonal wave that breaks down the formation of the south polar vortex. The application of the same methods used to study the south polar vortex in the 1980s to the north polar vortex in the 2000s enabled researchers to detect the differences in the formation of the two vortices. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. It is also worth noting that achieving optimal blow-up criteria in domains with infinite space requires alternative approaches. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Moreover, the proposed algorithm is generally applicable to other x-ray scattering off nuclear resonances and other temporary and energetic x-ray interferences with phase information available through time-domain measurements. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of maintaining phase information in real-time and frequency spectra, particularly for magnetic scattering off nuclei, where important information about a target can be lost within a few nanoseconds or microelectrons due to particle decay or displacement through beam interaction, highlighting the potential of our approach for recovering such lost information. Our approach has been openly shared for the scientific community to utilize, and the code can be found at https://github.com/ASAR-NKNI/xrd_mossbauer_fit. The experimental setup used in this study is also publicly available at https://github.com/ASAR-NKNI/Experimental_setup. The knowledge gained from this research can be applied to other interferences involving temporary and energetic x-ray states off targets that lose phase information over time. The relevant data and experiments have been deposited in the following locations: https://github.com/ASAR-NKNI/xrd_mossbauer_fit and https://github.com/ASAR-NKNI/Experimental_setup. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. This is especially evident when considering the evaluation of the norm of the pressure error in both two and three-dimensional settings. This occurs in addition to the known advantages of hybrid-dimensional approaches, including the precise reconstruction of the displacement field. This leads to a significantly simpler computation of the velocity field. This computation would otherwise involve a much more complex resolution of a mixed formulation if a blocking-blocking coupling was employed. This is in addition to the already mentioned advantages of using the Dirac-$\delta$ function to model blocking fractures, including the minimal amount of memory required to achieve accurate results. This is coupled with the ability to easily modulate the blocking fractures' permeability compared to the surrounding medium. This allows for a more realistic representation of certain natural phenomena, such as the interaction of blocking fractures with pressure and the flow of fluid along them. This interaction of the blocking fractures with pressure and the flow of fluid along them can now be accurately modeled, despite the distance between the blocking fractures and the observed effects being very large. This is due to the infinite permeability of the Dirac-$\delta$ function's support, along with the blocking fractures' ability to influence pressure and the flow of fluid along them without any decrease in distance. This leads to a significant improvement in the overall accuracy of the method, especially in the norm of the velocity field error.
