Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. We plan to expand on this research by applying these methods to existing studies within the cognitive sciences. Through this approach, we aim to provide useful tools and insights for the scientific community striving to make informed decisions about complex scenarios based on statistical models. We also explore potential opportunities to combine Bayes factor analysis with deep learning methods, such as neural density estimation, to enhance the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates. We emphasize the importance of open data management practices, revealing the raw data underlying research findings, to ensure the validity and reproducibility of research, particularly in the cognitive sciences, where Bayes factor analysis is commonly applied. We highlight the critical need for utility function independence from model parameters to make informed decisions about theories and models. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Evaluations based on various features show that the predicted indicators correlate strongly with discourse relations, suggesting that a significant portion of the variability among indicators is, in fact, due to the underlying discourse relations. Consequently, a classification system based on these predictions was employed to re-annotate the existing datasets, leading to a more precise alignment with the indicators that best characterize the English language. Furthermore, this new characterization is actionable, facilitating future improvements in the classification of discourse relations. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of predicting indicators for a deeper comprehension of the complex discourse relations within the English language, revealed through the emergence of various indicator categories from predictive models, beyond the limited examples typically observed in the literature. With DiscSense, this understanding can be applied to a broader set of datasets and scenarios, leading to a more refined and automated classification of discourse relations. Furthermore, the implicit grammar of English language has been revealed, making it a valuable resource for ongoing research in natural language processing, particularly in areas like generative models, where the representation of discourse relations remains a significant challenge. In the future, this research is expected to contribute to the development of more sophisticated sentence representations that capture the semantics of discourse relations, as well as the creation of natural language generators capable of producing diverse and semantically meaningful sentences. In the current form, the dataset can be utilized in classification tasks involving semantic discourse relations, as well as in evaluating the performance of models in predicting suitable indicators between sentences, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the model's performance. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases. The activation clipping project, along with the proposed protocol and techniques, is accessible via this link https://github.com/alexandresc/ActivationClipping-CCN. The code is licensed under the BSD 3-Clause License. The research presented was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and the Alberta Realities and Opportunities Fund. The data used was obtained from the MIOVision traffic dataset, which is publicly available via this link https://www.miovision.com/. The dataset is licensed under the Terms of Use of MIOVision Traffic Dataset. The design of the prototype was inspired by the work of Raucheberg et al. who utilized non-uniform data restriction to prevent memory errors in a linear regression model, and also discovered the positive impact of data restriction on model generalizability, which was subsequently confirmed through extensive experiments involving multiple datasets, models, and scenarios, and is thus considered a foundational finding. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our team has openly shared the code and vocabulary space at https://github.com/zhuyoshino/MSSE.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. We propose enhancing the model by introducing a simple diffusion process that takes into account areas with known previously infected populations and successfully recreate the observed spread of unrest in Santiago. By comparing the simulated results with actual disorder reports, we find that the revised model better aligns with the observed patterns of violence and destruction in Santiago. Furthermore, the model suggests that the most destructive episodes of violence were likely centered on specific subway stations in Santiago, whose identities remain unknown but can be identified by analyzing the model's parameters. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that urban spread models necessitate considering the movement of people across different geographic areas and highlight the potential benefits of using such models in planning and evaluating strategies for reducing the impact of violent disturbances in urban settings. Additionally, this study reveals that the ingredients of which areas experience violence and destruction during riots remain unclear and thus represents a crucial area for future research. We also propose that the method presented here could be applied to other notable instances of violence and unrest in urban settings around the world. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that despite its expanded capabilities, this algorithm addresses the containment issue with a depth of n, where n represents the depth of the input expression, whereas its character set recognition depth remains limited to a fixed, arbitrary but ascertainable integer. We also illustrate the efficacy of this algorithm by applying it to samples of regular expression containment assessment tasks. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Furthermore, we outline feasible experimental signatures for SHOWS, including the square root of chemical potential dependence in the tunneling spectrum and the anomalous transport properties. Nonetheless, the honeycomb-kagome SHOWS model also exhibits a variety of novel phenomena, such as the emergence of a Dirac cone in double-helix layered SHOWS and the possible realization of topological showboarding in this system. We expect SHOWS to serve as a springboard for a more in-depth exploration of square-root topological physics. Moreover, we propose possible materializations of SHOWS in 3D solid-state systems, thereby bridging the theoretical model with potential experimental realizations. Finally, we discuss the square-root topological properties in SHOWS within the context of their potential applications in quantum computing, such as the generation of topological showboarding and anomalous transport properties. We also propose that SHOWS can serve as a possible platform for realizing Majorana fermions in solid-state systems. We anticipate that the square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal model will fuel ongoing research into the novel physics exhibited by this phenomenon, as well as its potential utilization in quantum technologies. We further highlight the theoretical framework's versatility, which can be adapted to analyze related phenomena in other solid-state systems, such as SHOWS's analogs in 2D graphene and 1D chains. By integrating experimental and theoretical findings, we are confident that we have made significant progress towards demystifying the enigmatic envelope of Enghag's enzyme. In recognition of the showboarding phenomenon's intricate nature, we propose the introduction of an adjusted topological phase diagram that considers the square-root nature of the energy levels, which we term the "redox topology of the envelope of Enghag's enzyme". This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. A notable finding reveals that the current implementation yields overly conservative stability estimates. A proposed modification to the method demonstrates promising results, offering potential for improving the existing approach. A previous algorithm for recovering boundary data on an inaccessible segment, which works for the Helmholtz equation, is also evaluated and compared with the present method. A sample application to electromagnetic imaging is outlined. The research presents several potential extensions, including the use of gradient-based optimization and the extension of the model to account for material properties inside the confined domain. A notable limitation of the current approach is the requirement for initially smooth boundary data. A related issue is the presence of the Laplace operator in the integral equation, which may impede the method's extension to its own interface analysis within the realm of partial differential equations. A possible workaround is proposed, based on a dual formulation that retains the desired interface stability properties. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Moreover, our results indicate that FedSA is highly adaptable, able to leverage information from teachers who have trained on different languages, having varying levels of success. Additionally, we observed that FedSA remains robust in the face of significant data shortages. To facilitate further research, we are releasing the code and datasets associated with our experiments at https://github.com/Qianhewu/FedSA. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Our study also determines the lower and upper bounds of the rank growth from rational numbers to quadratic as well as cubic extensions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the majority of elliptic curves with a given discriminant have minimal rank zero in certain quartic and cubic fields, and nearly all of them have rank zero in a specific quadratic field, both as random curves and among optimally chosen curves for cryptographic purposes. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This report also presents three priority research areas and proposed observations for each. Ultimately, this study highlights the intricate connections between a planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere and the various processes that have formed Venus over time, with implications for our understanding of other planets and planets in general. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. It has also been determined that this component can serve other purposes, such as a polarization-controlled polarizer or a magnetic field sensor. This novel waveplate component demonstrates tremendous potential, prompting the necessity for further research into the properties of plasma in magnetic fields, especially under high powers and densities. This is the first proposal of such a component, and as such, there are opportunities to explore and optimize it further. This waveplate component can exist at normal incidence, yet the proposed research opportunities are similarly abundant for components functioning at other angles. It is also conceivable that this component's functionality can be achieved through other methods, yet the plasma-based approach offers the desired property of withstanding extremely high laser intensities. This approach is, however, initially challenged by the interaction of laser light and plasma particles, which can result in the distortion of the waveplate's properties over time. This issue needs to be addressed through further research into plasma interaction and possible stabilization techniques. It is also essential to experimentally verify the proposed properties and functionality of this component by creating a relevant setup that can successfully replicate the conditions required for the desired polarization transformation efficiency to be achieved. It is, however, anticipated that the efficiency of this waveplate component can be fine-tuned through adjustments to the plasma properties and the magnetic field strength. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. Our results also identify the parameters that yield optimal decoding performance. Furthermore, our symmetric error decoding results can be applied to the case of asymmetric errors when the underlying structure allows it. Our research is an initial step towards understanding the decoding of rank metric codes in more general settings. Our methods are compatible with combinations of symmetric and asymmetric errors, serving as a foundation for decoding algorithms employed in applications involving memory architectures. Our findings are also related to problems involving the security of cryptographic protocols based on rank metric codes. Our code decoding algorithms can be used in conjunction with other error-correcting codes, serving as a component in cryptographic protocols based on multiple code combinations. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. Furthermore, when the simulation parameters were altered, the accuracy of the best model was found to improve with time, despite the overall accuracy declining with time in all models. Finally, a significant difference was observed in the mass-prescription of WDM halos when using halo density, velocity, and position information, when compared to the standard model. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These results are compared to existing solutions obtained through other methods, demonstrating the accuracy and effectiveness of this novel numerical approach. 

Furthermore, our results highlight the significance of considering non-uniform angular velocity distributions, particularly in rotating neutron stars, and demonstrate that the angular velocity distribution can change in response to changes in the equation of state, mass loss or mass accretion, or stellar cooling, leading to eventual break-up into binary systems. 

In the context of neutron stars in binary systems, we have modeled the mass loss process from increasing mass accretion to eventual break-up, guided by observations of certain X-ray binaries, including V779 Tau, Vela X-1, and 4U 1538-52. We have also applied this approach to the well-documented supernova explosion SN 1987B, where the central element, likely a neutron star, reached an equilibrium configuration before exploding, and to which new observations can be fitted with greater precision. 

Finally, this method has the potential to be extended to binary star systems consisting of a stellar companion and a neutron star or black hole, where the close relationship between mass transfer and angular momentum transfer affects the evolution of the compact object, offering considerable potential for future research.

Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our approach has been found to outperform traditional active learning strategies, resulting in a 25% improvement in modeling performance at a fraction of the labeling expense. Our code and models are available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/NVIDIA/SelectiveLabeling. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of selective labeling and provides a practical solution to the document annotation challenge, enabling the wide-scale development of accurate models for real-world applications spanning many industries. Our findings also highlight the significance of accurately defining suitable domains for active learning, as this can result in a significant improvement in modeling performance – in our case, a 15% increase. Our proposed approach and associated data strategy are versatile and can be applied to a broad range of tasks and domains, making our research a valuable contribution to the active learning and automation communities. Our models have been trained using a substantial dataset consisting of over 60,000 documents, and the associated code has been made publicly available on the NVIDIA GitHub repository at https://github.com/NVIDIA/SelectiveLabeling. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We highlight the method's promise for future gravitational wave observations and emphasize the necessity of freely accessible, large datasets for training such models. Ultimately, this deep learning approach positions the community for a high-rate multi-messenger era of neutron star and black hole binary mergers. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Moreover, it highlights the importance of embracing non-physical interactions to boost urban diversity in the future. This study highlights the value of large-scale mobility data in monitoring the pandemic's impact on urban behavior and provides a viable framework for measuring diversity of urban encounters. This framework extends the limitations of current mobility indicators, offering valuable insights for policymakers, researchers, and practitioners seeking to enhance community resilience through targeted interventions in the era of COVID-19 and beyond. This is particularly crucial for developing strategies to revive vibrant urban diversity, a vital component of a city's economic and social vitality, according to the studies cited above. This study also paves the way for applying this framework in a wider context, evaluating the effectiveness of diversity-promoting interventions in urban settings. Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings. Consequently, details of high-mass stellar evolution will depend on various assumptions regarding the behaviour of accretion bursts, including the rate at which they apply pressure to the inner disk, whether objects can get stuck in the disk, and whether discs are turbulent or powered by magnetic winds. Additionally, the search for explanations for the Luminous Accretion Flares Equation will also need to consider the effects of massive stars on their surrounding environments. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Furthermore, we observed that the impact of vorticity on wave behavior becomes significant as the wave amplitude approaches 50% of its maximum possible value, normalization depth, as modeled using the Stokes wave profile. Our study contributes to a growing body of research, for which it seeks an optimal parameterization of the water's surface elevation. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for exploring more complex scenarios, such as bounded domains and realistic water levels. Moreover, it paves the way for investigating other Hamiltonian systems with weakly nonlinear behaviors under external influences. This approach is particularly valuable when the Hamiltonian formulation of a system is difficult to obtain directly. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. A demonstration of outdoor navigation in a more complex environment using multiple sonar sensors is also provided. This is a promising approach for future extension to a layered decision-making system using high-level maps for indoor navigation. This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time. The findings are demonstrated through computational simulations and confirmed by interpreting existing experimental data. The study's approach and findings are relevant to the analysis of complex systems in fields such as physics, biology, and finance. It introduces a new statistical method that can be applied to Gaussian random field models and offers an interdisciplinary perspective on the dynamics of these systems, inspired by theoretical concepts in modern geometry. It also presents an application in the study of the brain's neural dynamics, where it reveals an link between the structures of these systems and their cognitive functions, and provides an underlying framework for understanding the interplay between their internal time, geometry, and cognition. It presents an open-source computational tool that replicates the study's results and enables the customization of random field models for user-specific applications. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. Interestingly, our approach is the first to treat an invariant formulation of rotationally invariant L1-PCA through an iterative method. This method also provides a variational interpretation of the algorithm's results, offering yet another advantage. This research contributes to the understanding and application of rotationally invariant L1-PCA through meaningful examples and experiments. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This study demonstrates the feasibility of measuring the Meissener effect-induced centripetal force on atoms using atomic interferometry, and proposes a new method for measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors by accurately measuring atomic motion within a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Furthermore, it is possible to enhance the measurement accuracy by using a atomic interferometry system with increased sensitivity, to levels such as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This would entail using ultra-pure ensembles of atoms at near-zero temperature, and allows for the additional proposal of atom interferometry-based measurement of the expelled magnetic field gradient near a superconductor's edge, which could reach a precision of $10^{-16}$ Tesla per unit length. Finally, it is also possible to measure the expelled local magnetic field's very short-range variation, which occurs over a distance of approximately 10 micrometers, and could provide crucial information for understanding the Meissner effect's behavior at the atomic level. This research also explores the technical challenges involved in realizing such measurements in practice. In order to achieve this level of precision, it would be necessary to reduce external magnetic noise to levels as low as $10^{-14}$ Tesla per unit time, which is a challenging task, but one that is theoretically possible with anti-noise no noising techniques, or by using superconducting materials in sealed environments that prevent erosion of the surface expelling the magnetic field. This knowledge can be utilized in the search for non-zero expelling fields in certain types of superconductors, which has the potential to reveal the relationship between the Meissner effect and its expelling field gradients at the atomic level. This could, in turn, contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics governing superconductivity. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  The DynaSOAr framework is versatile and adaptable for other SIMD platforms in addition to NVIDIA GPUs.  Our benchmark data shows that DynaSOAr's execution speed can be adjusted to accommodate different problem sizes and types, thereby offering a high-performance computing solution that is both efficient and adaptable. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. These predictions and simulations demonstrate the material-specific model's capability to accurately simulate YSR states with particular attention to spin-orbit coupling effects. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Our study suggests that such defects could be stable at high temperatures, and that a more suitable model might involve larger antiferromagnetic ordering across multiple voids rather than just nearest neighbors.  The code utilized for these calculations is readily available within the VASP manual as an example set.  Overall, our findings indicate that carbon and nitrogen defects introduce a range of useful electric and magnetic properties to TiO2.  We propose that such a versatile material could be utilized in a variety of applications including photocatalytic splitting of water, fuel cells, and magnetic materials.  Our results also provide a basis for further investigation into defects involving other atoms.  We anticipate that such study could be accomplished through a combination of experimental and theoretical methods utilizing a range of codes including the VASP, PWSCF, and SIESTA packages.  We offer this research as a starting point for a variety of potential projects, and are confident that it will serve as a foundation for a range of scientific inquiries spanning materials science, physics, and chemistry. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor microchip was successfully integrated into a demonstration board, showing the ease of its application in complex systems. The research concludes with a comprehensive comparison of the proposed design against existing temperature sensor designs, highlighting its unique advantages, particularly in systems employing adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The design data is available at https://github.com/temperature-sensor-microchip. The temperature sensor microchip is suitable for various applications, including 5G base stations, server farms, and data centers. This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the development of the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids equipped with a connection has been introduced in [arXiv:2012.08447], the relationship between connections on principal bundles over Deligne Mumford stacks has been examined through the Atiyah sequence in [arXiv:2012.08442], and topological groupoid extensions were defined along with their correspondence to gerbes over topological stacks in [arXiv:2103.04560]. Moreover, the study provides a detailed analysis of the relationship between gerbes over Deligne-Mumford stacks and topological groupoid extensions, along with an investigation into central extensions of the fundamental groupoid of a stack. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the gerbe of units provides a connection to the gerbe of central extensions, and it also explores the notion of a monoidal gerbe over a monoidal stack. Lastly, the study offers an interpretation of Dolan Trimble's construction of a gerbe of pairs of linear operators and scalar fields on a linearised version of a stack, along with an extension of this construction to a gerbe of pairs of operators and scalar fields on an arbitrary stack. The study concludes by examining the relationship between gerbes of pairs of operators and scalar fields and the construction of linear logic from a linearised version of the stack. The study also discovers that 2-Heyting algebras arise from 2-linear logic, along with an interpretation of the elements of these algebras as pairs of operators and scalar fields on the stack. The study finally finds that the elements of these algebras also represent pairs of differential operators and their differentials on a distinguished connection on a principal bundle over the fundamental groupoid of the stack. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  Ultimately, it may facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the complex relationship between the mass distribution of cores and the masses of the stars they give rise to.  The studied cloud's specific characteristics, such as its remote location and lack of massive star formation, may have contributed to the observed pattern of mass growth among cores, which could be confirmed through the study of similar clouds. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. The validity of our "leverage rule" has been confirmed through calculations of stress distributions on model surfaces using the discrete element method. The stick-slip regime is characterized by increased friction, whereas the stationary regime is associated with lower curvature of Plateau borders and curvature that is more uniform. The curvature of Plateau borders becomes a critical factor in the absence of surface slippage, especially on rough surfaces with large asperities. The discovery of the stick-slip or stationary regimes on rough surfaces can serve as models for studying other complex phenomena, such as the formation of patterns in thin films and the sliding of particles off walls. The importance of surface curvature for the stick-slip or stationary regimes has been underscored by the findings of this study, which may serve as a basis for further research into the relationship between surface curvature and the curvatures of defects within liquid foams. The impact of surface roughness on the curvature of Plateau borders has been demonstrated through observations of the migration of border curvatures over time. The relationship between the energy of the system and the curvature of Plateau borders has been confirmed through the analysis of our data using the Ray-Pohlmeyer relation. The energy of the system also exhibits a direct relationship with the area of the system's surface and an inverse relationship with the curvature of the system's surface. The curvature of Plateau borders evolves over time in response to changes in the energy of the system following the displacement of a single plateau edge, as demonstrated through a combined analysis of stress measurements, visual observations, and numerical simulations. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. In particular, the look-ahead attention mechanism leads to a significant 8.1% reduction in BLEU score reversal error, and a 1.0 BLEU score gain on the standard NIST Chinese-to-English translation task. This achievement is achieved with only 1/8 the amount of target sentence reversal data commonly used in other research. Our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism is straightforward and efficient, and our results encourage future research on targeting complex dependencies within neural machine translation models. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our analysis of its parameters through the Markov chain Monte Carlo method reveals that it meets all the constraints posed by observational limits, which includes a host of dark energy parameters. Our computation of the future evolution of the universe within this model reveals that it will experience a transient period of accelerated expansion before being slowed by the bulk viscosity, ultimately leading to a destiny akin to that predicted by the dust model. Our estimation of the model's parameters through the Markov chain Monte Carlo method also enables us to determine the probable outcomes of the universe's future within this model. Our analysis of the model has been incorporated into the Cosmerger code, which simulates the merger of neutron stars and black holes. Our study reveals that the model accurately recreates the evolution of the Hubble parameter, the cosmic density, the deceleration parameter, the equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component, as well as the evolution of the cosmic viscosity coefficient. Furthermore, our analysis of the model has been applied to the analysis of certain gravitational waves signals generated during neutron star mergers. Our study suggests that the model enables a better understanding of the physics governing these mergers, by accurately predicting the formation of stars from the scalar perturbations of the cosmic density and the viscosity-driven deceleration parameter. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Our research demonstrates that J/ψ invisible decays offer a promising connection between particle and nuclear physics, and dark matter physics, with potential for significant progress in the near future. Our studies can be applied to other initial states, such as ψ'(2S), and offer extensions to visible J/ψ decays and other charmonium states. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, this approach provides a feasible solution for automatically detecting and counting individual cells in cancer diagnosis. Experimentation with a challenging real-world dataset showed that this approach outperformed existing models based on U-Net and attention mechanisms. Nonetheless, this approach is not without limitations, as it has been shown that certain datasets require a different strategy, but it is hoped that the W-shaped network will serve as a viable foundation for this challenging problem that needs further resolution. Experimentation with a real-world cancer cell counting dataset revealed that this approach exceeded the performance of U-Net and attention-based models. Nonetheless, it has also been demonstrated that certain datasets require a distinct strategy, but it is anticipated that the W-shaped network will serve as a starting point for further advancement. Moreover, to facilitate widespread adoption, the code for this approach has been made publicly available on a notable open-source platform known as GitHub. Furthermore, to enhance the scalability of this approach, a pioneering, publicly accessible dataset has been made available for the community to use in assessing the robustness of this model, along with a set of comprehensive guidelines for conducting rigorous experimentation. Ultimately, this approach has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to the pathology imaging community by providing a straightforward and automatic nucleus detection solution that is equally effective in non-scattered and fused NAC

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings. Finally, our result also expands on the characteristic zero results found in the works of T. A. Kramer, by incorporating the characteristics one, three, and five. It's worth noting that for the characteristic one, three, and five cases, our condition of representation isibility requires certain additional constraints. In the process, we have obtained key results related to the invariance of gamma factors, the categorization of irreducible generic representations, the partial Bessel function, and the smooth compact modulo center compactifications of the symplectic group Sp(2r)(F) and its dual group. These results are significant components of our proof and are valuable in their own right. In the case of a non-defining characteristic, especially characteristics one, three, and five, our categorization of irreducible generic representations relies on the analysis of gamma factors. Consequently, our result can be viewed as an extension of the works of T. A. Kramer. Moreover, our investigation of the partial Bessel function and the associated system of equations has been facilitated by the application of ultradiscrete Dunkl operator equations, which have been previously proven by I. Chou and which in turn rely on the findings of M. D. Kramer and T. A. Kramer. Additionally, our study of the symplectic group Sp(2r)(F) and its dual group involves the analysis of the ultradiscrete root system, which in turn involves the resolution of a certain type of equation known as the ultradiscrete Dunkl operator equation

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Consequently, VSSA appears poised to enhance elastography imaging, particularly in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement, and is worthy of further research. This study utilizes a 10 MHz ultrasound scanner but the proposed technique is scalable to other frequency ranges. This research demonstrates the capabilities of VSSA in improving lateral resolution and sampling frequencies in SA elastography, thereby paving the way for its use in other elastography imaging techniques. The proposed VSSA-beamformed elastography technique exhibits promising outcomes in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement, particularly at deeper imaging depths, and is therefore worthy of further investigation. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This is particularly useful for addressing decisions within interactive systems, as it allows the inclusion of predictive elements through the use of forward operators, which are capable of deriving new facts from existing ones. This framework is subsequently applied to the development of interactive systems, which we refer to as "dialogue schemata." These schema define possible conversations, guiding the system's response based on previous user inputs, ensuring that each step is a logical consequence of the information gathered so far. This approach provides a natural solution to the problem of proactive decision-making within interactive systems, as well as providing a guarantee of validity for the derived conclusions. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We construct this scalable solution by modifying the spectral algorithm that resolves the $k$-means problem, and in doing so, we discover a key relationship between coreset storage and the curvature of points relative to the target centers. Furthermore, our research introduces an innovative approach to handle stream dynamics by leveraging the concept of pseudocenters that serve as proxies for the underlying true centers, and we demonstrate how to maintain these pseudocenters through a series of stream updates by utilizing our coreset algorithm as a building block. We establish the efficacy and efficiency of our algorithm by proving the accuracy of its output and the narrowness of its used storage capacity. Ultimately, our algorithm yields results that are comparable to those obtained through optimal solutions in the standard setting of large datasets. We also establish lower bounds on required storage capacity in both stream and matrix settings, and these results demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm in both contexts. In addition, we present an illustrative application of our coreset algorithm in the context of dynamic streaming regression. We conclude the section by highlighting the main advantages and limitations of our research. We anticipate that our coreset algorithm will find utility in a broader spectrum of tasks and problems that involve dynamic data analysis, clustering, and curve fitting. We also emphasize the novel connection we discovered between coreset storage and the curvature of points relative to the target centers, a phenomenon we view as an interesting independent phenomenon worthy of further exploration in the future. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Furthermore, it proves to be robust in scenarios with significant differences in reward distribution. Our approach also facilitates policy learning from data, enabling the incorporation of historical trajectory information. Our results show that this approach outperforms flat policies in various settings, including those with complex dynamics, multiple pursuer agents, and varying observation mechanisms. Our hierarchical policy framework provides a versatile and optimized solution for a wide range of large-scale evasion games. Our code is available at https://github.com/hugobbier hierarchicalPEG.

synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our approach is called separate-but-shared (SBS) dynamics learning
and our results demonstrate that it efficiently extracts shared structure and
dynamics specific information, resulting in higher performance compared to traditional
single-share dynamics models. Our code is available at https://github.com/hulei001/sbs_dynamics_learning. Our approach and findings are valuable for the community working on
multi-task reinforcement learning with focus on dynamics learning. Our SBS approach
can be considered as a new baseline for such scenarios where tasks share
