We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We demonstrate how the ingredients of the Diagonal Lemma can be used to derive the unprovability of a specific statement within any formal system, thus mirroring the spirit of Tarski's Undefinability Theorem. Furthermore, we present a proof of Godel's first incompleteness theorem that is based on the contrast between the ability to quote or reference any statement within a formal system, as opposed to the limitation of being able to derive any statement that refers to itself. We also touch on the implications of these results for the concept of a self-referential statement, as well as the relationship between incompleteness and undecidability. Lastly, we outline some historical background and the key insights that led to the development of these theorems. We then proceed to explore various interpretations and their associated challenges, in addition to discussing some notable consequences that have been derived from these theorems, such as the possibility of constructing formally undecidable statements at any desired level of a given formal system, the limitation of any formal system to detecting its own inconsistencies, the relationship between these theorems and the fundamental properties of consistency, completeness, and decidability, as well as the potential applications of these theorems in related fields of study. We conclude by considering some of the Critiques and potential extensions of these theorems, in addition to examining some notable failed attempts to prove similar results about formal systems. We then move on to exploring some notable results that have been derived from these theoreorems, such as the capability to construct formally undecidable statements at any desired level within a given formal system, the limitation of any formal system to detecting its own inconsistencies, the restriction of consistency from a certain level within a formal system, as well as the properties of consistency, completeness, and decidability. We also examine the relationships between these theorems and some fundamental properties of formal systems, such as the capability to quote any statement within a formal system, the distinction between a statement that refers to itself and one that does not, as well as the possibility of constructing self-referential statements within a formal system

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Additionally, we derive the Cauchy operator's extension and apply these findings to establish the uniqueness of solutions to eigenvalue problems, specifically Du = λu and Hu = μu, within certain geometrically defined domains in R^n+1. Furthermore, these domains include the intersection of n geometric spheres. Lastly, we also address the uniqueness of solutions for the Dirac operator H given the domain's shape, given that the solution satisfies certain boundary conditions, specifically |u(x)| = f(x) and |u(x)| = g(x) for x belonging to the intersection of exactly two spheres. Futhermore, we also prove the uniqueness of solutions for the Dirac operator H given the domain's shape, given that the solution satisfies certain boundary conditions, specifically |u(x)| ≤ f(x) and |u(x)| ≥ g(x) for x belonging to the intersection of exactly two spheres. This research builds upon previous work by Shaw, which established the three balls theorem for monogenic functions within R^3+1 space. Nevertheless, the generalization presented in this paper supplants Shaw's results. The approach taken utilizes a different method than Shaw's, thereby providing an independently verifiable proof for the three balls theorem within R^3+1 space. The generalization achieved in this paper also extends the spectrum of values for which the three balls theorem holds, as well as extending Shaw's result to the R^n+1 space for any n. The operator technique employed in this research is analogous to the approach taken in a related problem in the plane, which was addressed by Hahn and Shapiro. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, because GANs tend to be noisy and dependent on specific training data, we regularized the model with an additional penalty term to enhance sampling consistency and stability. This led to an significant improvement in FID score, with a value of 25.1 in a tough MRI reconstruction task, indicating high sampling precision even without re-training the model. The proposed method cuts down memory consumption by integrating a multi-scale U-Net for conditional image synthesis, reducing required video memory by a factor of three without compromising on performance. The code for this framework is publicly available at https://github.com/liechao/WWGAN.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Consequently, we emphasize the importance of distinguishing between these invariant configurations and confusing them with other dynamical system properties. Additionally, we highlight the challenges and opportunities presented by fractional-order systems and the necessity of developing mathematical tools and methods tailored to their unique characteristics. Finally, we review the applications of invariant manifolds in the stabilization of dynamical systems and the security of fractional-order systems, with a focus on control and feedback control designs. We also discuss the challenges and promising areas of research in this field. We conclude by highlighting the potential benefits of invariant manifolds in the context of time-varying systems and multi-agent networks. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's small size, 0.54 parsecs in diameter, suggests it is a pliable bubble wall that is actively interacting with the surrounding medium, causing the void's boundaries to change over time. Another screen, named Screen D, was also discovered in this line of sight, however its distance could not be determined with the available data. Both screens, particularly the void-associated one, may serve as targets for future observations aimed at studying the evolution of the Local Bubble. Furthermore, the void-associated screen's small size and distinct velocity make it an suitable object for investigating the dynamic relationships within the interstellar medium, specifically the dynamics of the void boundaries. The research presented in this paper is an initial exploration of a complex subject, with many unresolved aspects, such as the exact nature of the screens and the surrounding medium, requiring further investigation. The necessary tools and methodologies for such studies are now in place, and the data analyzed here suggests many other screens in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 await discovery, offering a rich potential for future research. The same screening phenomena observed in this study will also likely influence future high precision searches for gravitational waves in pulsar observations. The techniques developed here can be applied to other pulsars, with shorter baselines, to discover screens in the interstellar medium, providing a detailed picture of the medium's dynamics on a large scale. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to unsupervised music soundwave generation using a conditional model incorporating auxiliary frequency features from the generated signal, resulting in more realistic outcomes compared to the original WaveNet. The proposed QPNet architecture provides a versatile framework suitable for various quasi-periodic audio generation tasks. The code for QPNet is available on GitHub at the address specified in the text. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this approach leads to an expansion of the known classical results regarding the invariance of shadows, as well as the specific case of algebras, encompassing both classical and non-classical manifestations. Hence, it encompasses and extends prior proofs involving the invariance of shadows, including those presented by the second author, Lipshitz, Schwede, and Weiss, alongside Shulman and Dyckerhoff. Moreover, it provides the bicategorical generalization of their respective arguments. In the process, it also establishes the equivalence between functors derived from THH and shadows in the context of monoidal categories, thereby establishing a connection between them. Ultimately, it builds upon this fundamental connection to demonstrate the Morita invariance of shadows. Given its underlying axiomatic nature, the theory of shadows is found to be applicable to any bicategorical framework, including but not limited to: topological, motivic, and orbital bicategories. By means of the shadow construction, it is also possible to extend the applicability of functors from THH to an even broader spectrum of categories, as it enables the extension of invariance properties, such as Morita invariance, to categories that would otherwise fall outside the scope of current THH definitions. Consequently, this leads to a more general and nuanced understanding of the topological Hochschild homology, as well as its underlying axioms, which are found to be equivalent to the set of properties currently axiomatized by THH. In the topological setting, this leads to a distinction between different versions of THH, alongside ETHH, SETHH, and OETHH, each corresponding to distinct categories of algebras and exhibiting its own unique characteristics. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that functors from THH are equivalent to functors derived from the shadow construction applied to the underlying orbit category, thereby establishing a direct connection between them. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced on GitHub, along with VGG-Sound Source which can be accessed through the project website.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to GCNs in Euclidean geometry but with significant productivity gains, demonstrating the versatility of its architecture. Furthermore, LGCN is a computationally efficient solution, requiring only a minimal increase in computational resources compared to standard GCNs. This paper is an extended version of the work presented in 'ICML 2021'. Experimental evaluations have been expanded and additional analyses conducted. A simplified version of the algorithm has been included, and the paper structure has been adjusted based on reader feedback. The code for LGCN is publicly accessible on GitHub at the address listed in the additional files section. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this method enables us to solve the inverse problem through the use of a regularization technique. The solution to the source term is obtained by applying the technique to the combined PDE and measurement data. A numerical example based on a 2D model confirms the feasibility of this method. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model can be applied to value
learning through a parameter estimation method based on the Tsallis entropy, which
enables us to generate empirically supported examples and animation tools. Overall,
our delay discounting model incorporates the complexities of impulsivity, offering
insights into its underlying mechanisms and potential uses in educational value
learning environments. Our software is available at https://github.com/Yuandong-Wei/Tsallis-DDM. This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  Furthermore, this choice yields a covariant formulation of the linearized massive gravity field equations with a clear connection to the original Fierz-Pauli approach.  The analysis also extends to the minimally coupled harmonic linearized massive gravity model. For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Furthermore, the canonical thermal equilibrium state is found to correspond to a loxodromic dynamics, whereas both the semiclassical and high-temperature approximations result in parabolic dynamics. Nonetheless, despite the loxodromic dynamics appearing complex, the associated thermal equilibrium state remains real, illustrating that the associated complex symplectic matrix is a true symplectic matrix. Moreover, the associated metaplectic operator, which is initially defined through a Taylor series expansion, is found to be equivalent to a loxodromic operator that is linked to the complex symplectic matrix via a canonical relationship, thereby shedding light on the operator's precise dynamics. Ultimately, this research uncover's the underlying dynamics of thermal equilibrium quantum states with quadratic Hamiltonians, laying bare the intricate relationship between the associated complex symplectic matrix, the metaplectic operator, and the resulting thermal properties. It is also demonstrated that both the semiclassical and high-temperature approximations entail a loss of quantum dynamics, resulting in classical parabolic dynamics. This study paves the way for an in-depth examination of both microscopic and macroscopic quantum dynamics governed by a quadratic Hamiltonian. This discovery is particularly significant for understanding the thermal equilibrium properties of microscopic and macroscopic quantum systems in relation to their associated classical dynamics. This research is a natural extension of previous findings related to both harmonic oscillators and their coupled systems. This class of quadratic Hamiltonians encompasses not only harmonic oscillators and coupled harmonic oscillators but also massive scalar fields, electromagnetic fields in a cavity, and charged bosons in a cavity among other systems. Thus, this research has far-reaching implications for the thermal properties of these diverse systems of quadratic Hamiltonians. This study is a more detailed exploration of the complex dynamics of thermal equilibrium quantum states in relation to their associated classical dynamics, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate relationship between the resulting thermal properties

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we highlight the implications of negative absolute temperature on the entropy of a two-level system and demonstrate its relationship with the Boltzmann distribution. Lastly, we examine the applicability of these concepts to quantum mechanics. Despite the fact that quantum mechanics and the energy-time uncertainty principle suggest that the concept of negative absolute temperature might be ephemeral, we argue that it is crucial knowledge for students to grasp, given the frequent observations of negative absolute temperature in quantum systems following perturbations. We also present simulated data illustrating the decay of negative absolute temperature in a two-level system over time. All the associated material can be found in the supplementary information provided with this report. We hope that the statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism we presented will be beneficial to students seeking a deeper understanding of the topic of negative absolute temperature. We also believe that the supplementary information we have made available may be useful as a teaching resource for university physics courses. In the appendix, we have included a discussion on the statistics of rarefied systems and the relationship between their phase space distribution and that of systems exhibiting negative absolute temperature. We have alternatively derived the Boltzmann distribution through time-reversal symmetry in the main text, and also explored the relationship between the entropy of a two-level system and the absolute temperature within the appendix. We have further illustrated the utility of these concepts by examining the negative absolute temperature observed in excited atoms following an initial drive. We have also developed a simulator that demonstrates the decay of negative absolute temperature over time following an energy drive. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we analyze the predictions for low-energy neutrino phenomena and propose distinguishable signatures in direct detection experiments for the dark sector components. Overall, the simplest scoto-seesaw model offers an integrated explanation for the "arithmetic" relationship between the neutrino mass scales, in addition to providing motivational insights for the study of dark matter at both low and high energy levels. The relevant theoretical and experimental aspects are explored in detail. The model also leads to a novel prediction for the $J_{\rm C}$ asymmetry in top quark production, offering a distinguishable signature for future particle colliders. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, the small mixing fraction we find in MoO$_2$ is sufficient to explain the incorrect prediction of a small moment at the Mo site in a previous study, which mistakenly ignored $e_g$ orbital occupation; rather, we find that the observed moment is explained by considering all $d$-orbital types and using the correct effective spin-orbit coupling. Similarly, our study suggests that the branching ratio for 5d Ru based oxides may have been inaccurately interpreted in the past due to $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, leading to an incomplete understanding of the underlying physics. Nonetheless, by accurately accounting for $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, the complex magnetic properties of these materials can be fully explained with a simple $d$-orbital based model. These findings are relevant to a wide range of transition metal oxides, including but not limited to Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, Ba$_2$IrO$_4$, RuO$_2$, MoO$_2$, and (Ca,Sr)RuO$_3$. The research demonstrates that while the 4d and 5d transition metal oxides share some similarities with 3d based materials, the larger spin-orbit coupling in these higher d shells can lead to fundamentally distinct physics resulting from interacting electrons, offering a compelling argument for exploring these materials within a unified orbital framework. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it highlights the significance of these findings in relation to genus-zero property predictions. Lastly, it presents an illustrative example utilizing genus-zero properties to analyze the quantum coefficients of a particular set of objects known as Witten's 3-point symbols. This leads to a conjecture regarding the form of these coefficients, which are otherwise unknown due to the limited data available in the genus-zero property database. This conjecture is supported by genus-one quantum coherence analysis and can be verified by genus-zero property proofs, which remain to be discovered. This research was initially presented at the 2014 Southeastern Lie Theory conference. It has since been expanded into a more comprehensive study. This expanded study has been categorized into two primary areas of investigation, which have been treated as two separate research endeavors, one by each author. The first author has exclusive rights to the conclusions drawn from genus-one coherence analysis, whereas the other author contributions are as follows: the second author contributed to the research on Witten's 3-point symbols, the third author contributed to the research on Witten's 3-point symbols and FJRW, and the fourth author contributed to the research on toric complete intersections. It is worth noting that this expanded research has been categorized into two separate areas of investigation, each with its own set of authors, although the original conference presentation credited the authors as a collective group known as the Southeastern Lie Theory Conference 2014 Participants. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a beginning step in medical GAN usage, presents a starting point for multiple interesting directions such as incorporating clinical information, developing a more efficient inverse mapping technique, and utilizing this approach for disease detection. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is particularly suited for
experienced professionals in the field of geosciences. A Windows version of
ViDaExpert is presented, and the application's underlying architecture is
discussed, along with guidance on publishing 3D visualizations. A Linux version
of the application is also available. The source code of ViDaExpert is
available at https://github.vdaexpert. A tutorial on creating a 3D scenario
with ViDaExpert is also provided. The application was initially developed for
the analysis of geophysical data, but it can be employed for any type of
multidimensional vectorial data. The research presented underwent testing on
various datasets, including a dataset with 500 objects, 20 features, and 5
classes, for which the application extracted relevant information and produced
an informative 3D visualization. The research is relevant to areas like
geophysics, mining, and agriculture, and the application's functionality can
be expanded through integration of machine learning models. The research and
application development underwent funding from the New Zealand Government.
